title: Volunteerism as a Catalyst for Socioeconomic Development in Algeria

detail.title: Volunteerism as a Catalyst for Socioeconomic Development in Algeria
detail.abstract:
Volunteerism in Algeria plays a complex role intersecting social cohesion, grass roots problem-solving, and economic support systems. This study examines initiatives such as Green Algeria and White Algeria, which address environmental restoration and healthcare access disparities, respectively, while contributing to human capital development and community resilience. These movements operate within cultural and religious frameworks that shape participation and motivation, highlighting the importance of integrating volunteer efforts into formal policy and institutional structures. Economic impacts are observed at local and national levels through market stimulation, skill acquisition, and service substitution, with potential to support diversification beyond traditional sectors. Social benefits include enhanced trust, reciprocity, and inclusive
identity formation, which strengthen collective capacity for sustainable development. Comparative analysis of global best practices suggests that strategic policy integration, capacity-building, legal protections, and technological coordination can improve volunteer sector effectiveness. Addressing regional disparities and embedding volunteerism within national development strategies could amplify its contributions to Algeria’s socioeconomic progress and international cooperation.

title: From Treasury Securities to Doctor of Osteopathic: The Macroeconomic Chain Linking Federal Reserve Debt Instruments, Tariff Policy, and Domestic Medical Labor in Post-Petrodollar America
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: From Treasury Securities to Doctor of Osteopathic: The Macroeconomic Chain Linking Federal Reserve Debt Instruments, Tariff Policy, and Domestic Medical Labor in Post-Petrodollar America

declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: This paper examines how U.S. monetary architecture—centered on Federal Reserve liabilities (“IOUs”)—interacts with tariff policy, reserve diversification into gold, and domestic human-capital responses. Using structured descriptive evidence (2010–2025) from Treasury TIC, IMF/WGC, and AAMC/AACOM/HRSA/CMS series, we document three co-movements: (i) China’s gradual rotation from U.S. Treasuries into gold; (ii) episodic equity–gold divergence around tariff and debt-ceiling events; and (iii) a regional substitution toward domestically trained physicians (DO capacity) where foreign inflows of medical labor have been constrained. We explicitly treat the idea that market drawdowns facilitate a portfolio rotation toward hard assets (“policy choreography”) as a hypothesis, and report alternative explanations (liquidity cycles, term-premium repricing, global risk). We conclude that rising reliance on human capital—through STEM, healthcare training, and technical education— functions as a partial offset to declining external demand for U.S. paper, consistent with a transition from petrodollar-anchored finance to a more diversified, skill-anchored solvency.

title: Beyond Eurocentrism: Sovereign Interoperability as a Decolonial Project in International Relations
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Beyond Eurocentrism: Sovereign Interoperability as a Decolonial Project in International Relations
detail.abstract: This article develops the Theory of Sovereign Interoperability as a decolonial project for International Relations, overcoming traditional Eurocentric frameworks. Through the analysis of BRICS cooperation, we demonstrate how this approach explains Global South collaboration forms based on informal coordination, sovereignty preservation, and strategic pragmatism. The study employs qualitative methodology with case analysis of the New Development Bank and vaccine diplomacy during the COVID-19 pandemic, revealing how sovereign interoperability constitutes both an analytical tool and an act of epistemological decolonization. The results evidence that this framework overcomes the limitations of realism, liberalism, and constructivism in explaining cooperation among diverse states that maintain strategic autonomy. We conclude that the theory represents an advance toward theoretical pluralism in IR, offering conceptual tools to understand the dynamics of an emerging multipolar world from non-Western perspectives.

title: U.S. Agricultural Exports to Southeast Asia – Recent Market Dynamics & Emerging Pathways Insights for Small and Mid-Sized American Producers
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: U.S. Agricultural Exports to Southeast Asia – Recent Market Dynamics & Emerging Pathways Insights for Small and Mid-Sized American Producers
detail.abstract: This white paper analyzes the recent dynamics of U.S. agricultural exports to Southeast Asia, focusing on Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Drawing on data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service (ERS) and Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS), it examines export composition, tariff structures, competitive positioning, and evolving market pathways across modern retail, foodservice, and processing sectors. The findings indicate a gradual shift from bulk commodities toward consumer-oriented and ingredient-based products, supported by urbanization, income growth, and the rise of e-commerce. For small and mid-sized American producers, opportunities lie in aligning export strategies with certification standards, retail and digital networks, and regional partnerships. These developments underscore Southeast Asia's growing importance to U.S. trade diversification and resilient agri-food supply chains.

title: The Perils of Bilateral Sovereign Debt
affiliations: International Monetary Fund and McMaster University - Faculty of Social Sciences

detail.title: The Perils of Bilateral Sovereign Debt

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the interaction between private and official sovereign debts. We develop a quantitative sovereign default model featuring a senior creditor with whom borrowing terms are negotiated. We use this model to evaluate implications of the emergence of new official lenders not bound by the Paris Club framework. The dynamics of bilateral bargaining lead the government to issue more market debt, raising default risk and creating welfare losses. This relational overborrowing effect arises in the model due to an endogenous cross-elasticity of bilateral terms to market debt, which can be assessed in practice to evaluate new forms of bilateral sovereign debt.

title: The Role of a Stabilizing Expenditure Rule in Fostering Macro-Fiscal Stability
affiliations: Warsaw School of Economics (SGH), Ministry of Finance , Warsaw School of Economics (SGH), International Monetary Fund (IMF), , International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and Warsaw School of Economics (SGH)

detail.title: The Role of a Stabilizing Expenditure Rule in Fostering Macro-Fiscal Stability

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The paper investigates the properties of Poland’s Stabilizing Expenditure Rule (SER) in the context of economic governance reform in the EU. The analysis uses a granular macroeconometric model (Chmura et al., 2024) that incorporates heterogeneous fiscal multipliers across expenditure items and endogenous tax bases. This novelty supports emprically-grounded simulations to analyze the impact of adverse shocks on output, fiscal balances, and debt dynamics, including through the binding expenditure rules and potential shifts in the composition of expenditures. Our results show that the SER generally ensures lower fiscal deficits (and debt path) than policies that only target the compliance with the Stability and Growth Pact (SGP) thresholds. This is because of the inherent corrective mechanism built in the SER that requires a tightening of fiscal stance when rules are breached. The SER is shown to have counter-cyclical properties, although the extent depends also on the parameters in the correction mechanism.

title: Behind Schedule? Assessing Global Developments in the Provision of Economic Statistics

detail.title: Behind Schedule? Assessing Global Developments in the Provision of Economic Statistics

keywords: timely dissemination of key macroeconomic and financial data

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We introduce a novel monthly index to measure developments in the provision of official economic statistics based on publicly disclosed observance records of subscribers to the IMF Data Standards Initiatives -- the IMF's policy framework to promote the timely publications of macroeconomic and financial data. While data is typically published in a timely manner, we document a notable decline in timely data releases since 2017. Persistent challenges in fiscal data dissemination, divergent trends in AEs and EMEs, and regional differences contribute to these dynamics. The overall decline also mirrors other global governance trends and the public disclosure of economic data tends to get less timely for some economies during turbulent periods. Strained resources devoted to statistical services can help rationalize. Through empirical applications, we demonstrate that these newly constructed indices contain predictive information for fiscal outcomes and economic downturns. Our findings demonstrate that while the Initiatives successfully promote the timely release of key macroeconomic and financial data, maintaining robust data dissemination requires sustained institutional capacity and adequate resource provision, especially during periods of distress when timely information is most crucial to support resolving macroeconomic imbalances and market disequilibria.

title: Price of Intelligence
affiliations: and Yale University

detail.title: Price of Intelligence

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Leading AI firms claim to prioritize social welfare. How should firms with a social mandate price and deploy AI? We derive pricing formulas that depart from profit maximization by incorporating incentives to improve welfare and reduce labor disruptions. Using US data, we evaluate several scenarios. A welfarist firm that values both profit and welfare should price closer to marginal cost, as efficiency gains outweigh distributional concerns. A conservative firm focused on labor-market stability should price above the profit-maximizing level in the short run, especially when its AI may displace low-income workers. Overall, socially minded firms face a trade-off between expanding access to AI and the resulting loss in profits and labor market risks.

title: Trade Dynamics in Sovereign Debt Crises
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Strategy Policy and Review Department, International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Research Department, University of Wisconsin-Madison and Keio University

detail.title: Trade Dynamics in Sovereign Debt Crises

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Sovereign debt restructurings can have large impacts on trade, with a significant compression of imports and a more ambiguous effect on exports. We show that the magnitude of that impact depends on whether restructurings preempt a default or take place after payments have been missed, with the latter associated with longer and deeper crises. Import compression is significantly higher following post-default restructurings, which also tend to be associated with higher exports relative to preemptive restructurings. This is consistent with the need for a larger external adjustment following a default. We also show how the effect varies across types of goods, and a larger impact when initial aggregate domestic demand in the debtor’s economy is high.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Lowering South Africa’s Inflation Target
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF)  and International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal Affairs Department

detail.title: Macroeconomic Effects of Lowering South Africa’s Inflation Target

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper explores the macroeconomic implications of lowering the inflation target in an Emerging Market such as South Africa using the IMF’s Global Integrated Monetary and Fiscal model (GIMF). Model-based simulations indicate that lowering the inflation target from 4.5 to 3 percent, as recently announced by South Africa’s central bank, may entail moderate near-term output costs (measured by the so-called “sacrifice ratio”), while leading to medium-term output gains and lower borrowing costs. The near-term costs critically depend on the credibility of the central bank, which determines the speed with which agents adjust their inflation expectations. Specifically, output costs are lower when inflation expectations adjust more rapidly following the announcement of the new target by the central bank. Similarly, higher sensitivity of risk premia to the announcement of a lower inflation target can further reduce these costs. Concurrent fiscal consolidation can help support the disinflation process and lower the marginal sacrifice ratio.

title: The Labor Market Returns to Delaying Pregnancy
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago, Aarhus University and Royal Holloway, University of London

detail.title: The Labor Market Returns to Delaying Pregnancy

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 25-22
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the extent to which delaying pregnancy mitigates the impact of children on women's labor market outcomes. We leverage quasi-random variation in the incidence of pregnancy in a setting where women intend to delay having children by using long-acting reversible contraceptives. While most women successfully delay pregnancy, some have unplanned pregnancies. Analyzing linked health and labor market data from Sweden, we find that unplanned pregnancies halt women's career progression resulting in income losses of 20% five years after the unplanned pregnancy. Using pregnancy as an instrument for birth in a dynamic treatment effect framework, the detrimental effects of unplanned children are larger for younger women and women enrolled in education-indicating that unplanned first births are particularly disruptive early on when women are investing in their human capital. In contrast, we find smaller impacts of unplanned pregnancies for women who are already mothers. Similarly, when we estimate the impact of first births identified from quasi-random success of fertilization procedures, we find smaller impacts of children among women who intend to get pregnant. These findings highlight the critical role of pregnancy intentions and timing in determining the economic consequences of motherhood.

title: A Search-Based Theory of Mergers and Acquisitions
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: A Search-Based Theory of Mergers and Acquisitions

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a search-based theory of mergers and acquisitions with heterogeneous firms and endogenous search complementarities. We use this model to understand how merger incentives and the firm size distribution interact. In equilibrium, search costs and entry rates determine search intensities and shape the distribution of market power. We derive the law of motion of the firm size distribution, provide closed-form solutions, and solve for endogenous search efforts. Finally, we derive the aggregate welfare function and show how our framework can be used to simulate the impact of various antitrust policies. In particular, antitrust policy can have large effects on welfare due to the existence of multiple equilibria.

title: Unpacking the Current Surge in Sick Leave: Insights from Spanish Administrative Data
affiliations: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC), Ispra, Italy and European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC), Ispra, Italy

detail.title: Unpacking the Current Surge in Sick Leave: Insights from Spanish Administrative Data
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the factors contributing to the current sharp rise in sick leave prevalence occurring in many developed countries, using Spain as a case study. Using individual-level Social Security data for 2018-2023, we examine the evolution of days on sick leave across worker and job characteristics and implement an Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to quantify each factor's contribution to the increase. We document a 36% increase in the share of days on sick leave, a trend common to a wide range of demographic and job characteristics. Observable factors such as population ageing, increasing employment opportunities, or longer healthcare waiting times account for only about 26% of the rise. Short-and longterm sick leaves show distinct patterns: over 60% of the rise in short absences is attributable to falling unemployment, consistent with behavioural responses in periods of economic expansion, whereas 90% of the growth in long absences remains unexplained by observable factors. Musculoskeletal and mental health conditions account for the largest increase, with mental health being particularly important for the under 40, explaining between 35% and 56% of the rise in days lost. Regional panel data models show that long-term mental and musculoskeletal sick leave rates are significantly associated with increased work stress and pain-related limitations, suggesting that genuine health deterioration is contributing to the surge in long-term sick leaves. Our results highlight a concerning deterioration in mental health among the younger workforce with broader consequences for both workers, employers and the welfare system.

detail.abstract: This study offers a bibliometric review of healthcare service quality, a field that has become increasingly important in the literature. We analyzed 3932 research articles published from 2000 to 2024 extracted from the Scopus database through employing VOSviewer and Biblioshiny software. Our analysis attempted to reveal patterns in this research area, such as the most prolific and influential writers, level of collaboration among authors, preferred outlets for publications, themes that dominate and evolve in the field. The results indicate that the United States and the United Kingdom rank as the largest contributors to literature on quality in health care services and Health Services Research and International Journal for Quality in Health Care emerging as the most productive journals. The most important contributors were Crabtree B.F. and Rubenstein L.V., among others. The study indicates a strong and increasing publication trend portraying an ongoing interest and growth in the research of health care service quality. This research has important implications for researchers as well as practitioners who are interested in this important healthcare area.

title: Algorithmic Mortality and Grammatical Immortality: A Theory of Civilizational Regeneration
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Algorithmic Mortality and Grammatical Immortality: A Theory of Civilizational Regeneration
detail.abstract:
"The Eunoia Path" proposes a new framework spanning civilizational studies, systems philosophy, and organizational theory: the "Transmissible Algorithm".

The author argues that the true longevity of a civilization does not depend on institutions, borders, or power structures, but on a more implicit capability – the continuous updating of **Judgment Grammar**. The life cycles of civilizations, enterprises, and even individuals are essentially cycles of Tension between algorithms and grammar: algorithms are responsible for Execution and efficient operation, while grammar is responsible for judgment and symbolic generation. When algorithms age and grammar becomes depleted, civilization falls into entropy and semantic rupture; when grammar is recompiled, civilization can breathe and revive.

The text is divided into eleven chapters, from "Civilizational Dynamics" to "Sovereign Actor Retirement", systematically elaborating how civilizations achieve energy cycles, ethical Tempo Tuning, and judgment regeneration through the Field-Shi Model and Eunoia Path rules. The author further proposes the proposition that "AI is the grammar abstractor of civilization", pointing out that artificial intelligence does not replace human judgment, but is an extension mechanism for civilization’s self-reflection and Grammar Encapsulation. When AI co-governs with humans, with humans defining values and AI maintaining structure, civilization can acquire a "Second Memory System". At the organizational level, the author uses enterprises as a microcosm of civilization, pointing out that the essence of "longevity" is not business continuity, but grammatical re-executability – that is, the organization can still answer "why it exists". At the civilizational level, history is redefined as "grammar migration history": when algorithms rise, the world accelerates; when algorithms retreat, the world echoes; and when grammar endures, civilization does not die.

The conclusion returns to the philosophical mother theme: "Let algorithms retire, and let civilization continue to breathe."

The immortality of civilization lies not in the continuation of power, but in the continuous understanding of meaning; the immortality of the individual lies not in their name being remembered, but in their Judgment Grammar still being in operation. When a society can continuously recompile its grammar, it possesses the ability for self-evolution. This book therefore proposes a new civilizational paradigm: Algorithms may retire, grammar should be ever-new; As long as there is breath, civilization will not die.

title: Toward a Sustainable Cost Optimization Model for Humanitarian Supply Chains in Disaster Response

declarations.funderStatement: this research did not receive funding.

detail.abstract: This study addresses a critical gap in humanitarian logistics research: the lack of systematic, practical cost optimization models tailored to the chaotic and uncertain conditions of disaster response. While prior work has emphasized responsiveness and coordination, high operational costs continue to hinder the efficiency and reach of humanitarian aid. This research explores strategies that balance cost efficiency with delivery speed, such as the "leagile" approach that blends lean and agile principles. It examines best practices in inventory management, network design, and technology use, while also analyzing lessons learned from past failures. The study ultimately proposes a sustainable framework that enables humanitarian organizations to optimize costs without compromising the timeliness or quality of aid— ensuring that limited resources can reach more people in need during crises.

title: Metaverse Mediation: Balancing Business and Artistic Needs (A)
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Metaverse Mediation: Balancing Business and Artistic Needs (A)

publicationDetails.journalName: Darden Case Collection

detail.abstract:
Set during the Screen Actors Guild and Writers Guild of America strikes in the 2020s, this fictional case follows recent MBA graduate Emma Collins, a new employee at the MuseMeta music and AI studio. MuseMeta is designing a metaverse concert for the best-selling pop group SWOT, with the opening act being the company's AI-generated singer, Ava. Unfortunately, Ava's performance has generated conflict, not just among music fans divided by AI's impact on art, but with a human artist who had previously opened for SWOT's tours. Worse still, pressure to churn out a song addressing this crisis has led to internal tension with Ava's creative designer. While Collins has a strong business background, she's never navigated the unique challenges of working with creatives, and especially not in a space as divisive as AI music. Students will explore conflict mediation in the dynamic world of virtual concerts and AI collaborations, consider what name, image, and likeness means in an increasingly AI-generated culture, and ask how to balance the world of business with the world of art. This case is designed for MBA and Executive MBA students enrolled in courses that explore the intersection of business strategy, creativity, and technology. Students address not only questions of reputation and brand management, but connect quantitative reasoning (audience analytics, engagement metrics) with qualitative human understanding (authenticity, empathy, artistic voice). It is well-suited for classes in Media and Entertainment Business, Storytelling with Data, Technology and Innovation Strategy, Leading Creative Teams, and AI Ethics. Across all contexts, the case equips future leaders to confront one of the most urgent questions facing business and society today: How can organizations harness AI for innovation while preserving the integrity and meaning of human creativity?

Excerpt

Metaverse Mediation: Balancing Business and Artistic Needs (A)

Emma Collins stepped into MuseMeta, a music and artificial intelligence (AI) studio that brimmed with holographic displays and AI assistants. Based in Austin, Texas, the firm specialized in developing all types of music tours, including live, remote, digital, and metaverse-based experiences. The air buzzed with excitement as Collins was greeted by the team of passionate creators working on a metaverse concert for the best-selling pop band SWOT's new tour. Ava, an AI-generated singer, stood as the centerpiece of the studio's promotional display. She would debut as the opening act in the metaverse performance. Ava was designed using a method similar to what Eline Van der Velden at Particle6 Productions had used to create AI actress Tilly Norwood, as well as what Factor New and Brandon Le had employed to create AI rapper FN Meka, known for such songs as “Speed Demon.”

Collins was absolutely floored by the display. As she reflected, she mused, “I'd learned about this concept only a couple years back, and the progress of this beta test is truly remarkable. That they've managed to incorporate the likenesses of so many celebrities into Ava is astonishing. Even more so that they'd authorize the use of their images this way.”

Collins was a recent MBA graduate, and she was elated to work in the entertainment industry after graduation. She had never worked with artists before but was exceptionally eager to do so. Previously, she had worked as a media and entertainment consultant at McKinsey & Company (McKinsey) in its New York office. She was excited for a change of scenery and to be part of something epic.

title: Minimum Wage and Employment
affiliations: and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Minimum Wage and Employment

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Most European countries have a single national minimum wage. An increase in minimum wage implies shocks of different magnitudes to sectors and subnational regions. Using sectoral and regional variations of minimum wage to average wage ratios in European countries, we estimate the dynamic and heterogeneous treatment effects of minimum wage changes on employment through local projections and generalized random forests. We find that the average employment effects of minimum wage increases tend to be negligible in the short term but negative in the medium to long term. The employment effects are heterogeneous in gender, age, the size of the minimum wage increase, and the minimum wage to average wage ratio. Minimum wage increases appear to have a threshold effect on employment at the sectoral level. The employment effects become negative when the minimum wage is above 35 percent of the sectoral average wage.

title: A MILP framework for optimizing decarbonization pathways in industrial plants: Case study of a steel hot rolling mill
affiliations: TU Wien, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Vienna University of Technology, Vienna University of Technology and Vienna University of Technology

detail.title: A MILP framework for optimizing decarbonization pathways in industrial plants: Case study of a steel hot rolling mill
detail.abstract: Long-term decarbonization of industrial energy systems requires strategic investment decisions across multiple planning periods, as complete transformation cannot be realized immediately but must be strategically phased considering technological uncertainties, volatile energy markets, and evolving policy frameworks. To address this challenge, generation expansion planning (GEP)—a well-established approach for long-term electricity infrastructure optimization—offers a suitable methodological foundation. This study adapts the GEP framework to develop a site-level optimization model for industrial decarbonization pathways using mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). We demonstrate the approach through application to a steel hot rolling mill in Styria, Austria, where natural gas-fired furnaces currently reheat steel slabs prior to rolling. Two alternatives are evaluated: a hydrogen retrofit furnace and an induction furnace. Further, an extended energy system allows the integration of electrolyzer, hydrogen and battery storages, PV, and carbon capture plants. The MILP-based transformation planning tool determines cost-optimal investment and operation pathways under various techno-economic scenarios. Results show a positive correlation between the level of emission reduction and total costs, with sharply rising marginal abatement costs for near-complete decarbonization. The findings also show that even high CO2 price assumptions do not sufficiently incentivize substantial system transformation. Emission limits or strong regulatory incentives are necessary to trigger significant decarbonisation. However, the integration of a carbon capture plant enables substantial CO2 reductions at comparatively low additional cost. Across all scenarios, fuel and energy costs represent the dominant share of total expenditures, whereas investment costs contribute significantly less. The analysis shows a consistent reliance on a diverse portfolio of technologies, both for heat supply and for energy procurement. This diversity enables electricity price arbitrage, which significantly improves overall cost efficiency. Further, the hydrogen pipeline emerged as a crucial element as its absence led to substancial increase to total costs.

title: Navigating a Down Round in Venture Capital: GoStage Ventures (SPANISH)
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and Independent

detail.title: Navigating a Down Round in Venture Capital: GoStage Ventures (SPANISH)

publicationDetails.journalName: Darden Case Collection

detail.abstract:
This is a Spanish translation of the August 5, 2024 version of UVA-F-2082. GoStage Ventures Fund LP (GoStage Ventures), a global venture capital firm, has a portfolio company, Motocredible Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (MotoSpin), that is pursuing a much-needed Series B financing round. MotoSpin was founded in Mumbai, India, to create a trusted and transparent online marketplace for pre-owned scooters, motorcycles, and electric vehicles (EVs). After several months of fundraising and hundreds of potential investor meetings, MotoSpin received a term sheet for a Series B financing round from ONE Capital, a large US-based impact fund. The problem for MotoSpin and GoStage Ventures is that the proposed Series B round valuation is at a 50% discount to the previous Series A round, creating a down round. In addition to the issue of the lower valuation, the ONE Capital term sheet proposed changes to many of the previous Series A round terms. Atiksh King, a vice president with GoStage Ventures, must decide how to respond to the proposed Series B financing. The case is appropriate for use in a first-year or second-year MBA course as well as an undergraduate business school elective that addresses venture capital, early-stage deal terms, and pricing of investment rounds in venture capital. Students should be familiar with venture capital financing in general before tackling this case. This case could also be used in an entrepreneurship class to illustrate how founders should think about term sheets, issues related to financing rounds, and how terms agreed to in a previous round can impact a subsequent financing round.

Excerpt

Navegar una ronda a la baja en capital de riesgo: GoStage Ventures

En un cálido y ventoso día de agosto de 2019, mientras Atiksh King, vicepresidente de GoStage Ventures Fund LP (GoStage Ventures), salía de un café en Powai, Bombay, India, y regresaba a su oficina, aún reflexionaba sobre el correo electrónico que había recibido. Se trataba de una propuesta de financiamiento Serie B para una de sus empresas en cartera, Motocredible Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (MotoSpin). ONE Capital, un gran fondo de impacto con sede en Estados Unidos, había presentado una hoja de términos (term sheet) para una inversión de $4,5 millones que le daría a la empresa el financiamiento tan necesario para sobrevivir y escalar. Aunque esto debería haber sido una buena noticia, había un problema con la valuación y las condiciones sugeridas. El nuevo inversionista proponía una inversión de $4,5 millones con una valuación previa a la inversión (pre-money) de $15,2 millones, más de un 50 % de descuento respecto de la valuación posterior a la inversión (post-money) de $33 millones de la Serie A en la que GoStage Ventures había participado previamente. Además, los términos planteados eliminarían ciertos derechos de inversión que GoStage Ventures había recibido como parte de su inversión Serie A en MotoSpin. Habría sido fácil para King rechazar de plano esta hoja de términos dados los problemas que generaría, pero MotoSpin llevaba varios meses buscando capital y no había encontrado muchos interesados. King y sus socios en GoStage Ventures estaban preocupados por invertir más que su participación pro rata en MotoSpin debido a la alta concentración que el Fondo II de GoStage Ventures tenía en este único negocio (aproximadamente el 10 % del Fondo II estaba invertido en MotoSpin).

Mientras King cruzaba la calle, pensaba: “Si GoStage Ventures rechaza esta hoja de términos propuesta, ¿quién aportará el capital para mantener a MotoSpin en funcionamiento, y sobre todo para ayudarla a crecer?”. Otro asunto era que la inversión total en MotoSpin era la mayor de la que él había sido responsable en GoStage Ventures, y le preocupaba cómo se vería reflejada esta situación en su reputación personal. ¿Verían otros su contribución a la empresa y al desempeño del fondo de manera negativa si GoStage Ventures tenía que depreciar en un 50 % el valor de su participación en MotoSpin? ¿Se le tendría en cuenta en su contra cuando llegara el momento de evaluarlo para un ascenso? ¿Y qué impacto podría tener semejante depreciación en el desempeño del portafolio del Fondo II justo cuando GoStage Ventures estaba comenzando reuniones con socios limitados (limited partners), también denominados “socios comanditarios”, tanto actuales como potenciales, para recaudar capital para el Fondo III?

King necesitaba reflexionar seriamente y elaborar una recomendación que pudiera compartir con sus colegas junto con la noticia. ¿Debería proponer que GoStage Ventures aceptara la hoja de términos y cerrara rápidamente, dada la falta de otros inversores? ¿Debería intentar negociar una mejor valuación y mejores condiciones, corriendo el riesgo de que el nuevo inversionista decidiera retirarse de la operación? ¿Debería proponer su propia hoja de términos con la valuación de la ronda Serie A y conservar los términos preferenciales, aun aceptando la elevada concentración que el Fondo II tendría en MotoSpin, o debería rechazar la hoja de términos para no perder tiempo valioso y seguir buscando capital con otros inversores? King no esperaba con entusiasmo esta conversación con sus socios. Al doblar la esquina hacia su edificio de oficinas, sabía que su recomendación afectaría no solo a MotoSpin, sino también a su posición dentro de la empresa.

Reversing Sickle Cell Disease: A Crisp Deal?

Carmen Jones, principal at White Lotus Ventures (White Lotus), a venture capital firm in the biotechnology (biotech) industry, pondered the latest deal the firm was considering. It had recently closed a $700 million fund and was evaluating several early-stage drug development companies. One of Jones's colleagues had introduced her to Switch Infinity Therapeutics (Switch), a firm that proved increasingly interesting the more she learned about it. Switch was utilizing CRISPR gene-editing technology for a gene therapy to treat sickle cell disease (SCD), a major cause of death and disability in people of African descent. While this treatment had the potential to be both incredibly impactful and lucrative, it was a new therapy built on new technologies that carried a lot of risk, and investment in it would take a large portion of the capital in the new fund.

Gene Therapy

Among the many applications of gene therapy, one of the most promising was gene editing, which involved making a targeted change in the DNA of an organism. The first gene-editing technologies, pioneered toward the end of the 20th century, relied on “programmable nucleases,” meaning proteins that could modify DNA. These gene-editing technologies operated via a protein complex that first identified the DNA site to be edited, then created a double-stranded break in that specific location. Finally, natural processes within the cell repaired the DNA to complete the editing process (Figure 1). These techniques had significant limitations based on the types of alterations that could be made, the locations on the host's DNA that could be targeted, the specificity and accuracy of the edits, the length of DNA to be edited, the complexity of the design, and the process of performing the edit itself. In these systems, the protein whose job it was to modify the DNA had to be specifically created to recognize a particular DNA sequence and perform each instance of editing. This is why these DNA-cutting proteins, or nucleases, were referred to as programmable.

Cybersecurity in the Post-AI Era

Cybersecurity (or just security, as it's called in tech and as we'll call it in this note) is no longer a niche responsibility managers can hand off—it's become a core, strategic function in every company. While it's part of tech at large, security continues in many ways as a domain unto itself. The fundamental difference between security and the rest of tech is its adversarial nature: With most tech activities, your primary user is the customer and you're trying to help them; with security, you have adversaries and you're trying to impede them.

Although just about everything in tech (e.g., users online, computing power, networking capacity, and profits) moves “up and to the right” (meaning it shows steady improvement over time), security is a notable exception. detail.abstract: Continuation funds (CFs) are private equity structures in which a manager raises a new fund to purchase assets from their existing fund. This structure has surged in popularity, from five funds in 2018 to 130 in 2024. We use a hand-collected sample of 472 CFs to test a model in which heterogeneous preferences drive CFs. detail.abstract:
Whether formally or informally, we're all managing projects and refining products. Neither project management nor program management is going anywhere, and every general manager should be familiar with the fundamentals of both, important distinctions between them, and how they interact with and complement each other. In this technical note, readers will learn which approach works best under conditions of certainty or uncertainty, how to charter a project and a product, how to strategically minimize waste, and, importantly, how to manage for outcomes. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this note is taught in the second-year “Digital Product Management” course; it would also be suitable in a module introducing product or project management.

Excerpt

Project Management Versus Product Management

Whether formally or informally, we're all managing projects and refining products. Neither project management nor program management is going anywhere, and every general manager should be familiar with the fundamentals of both. After reading this note, you will be able to

analyze a given endeavor in terms of its certainties versus uncertainties, particularly those related to outcomes and deliverables;

minimize waste by simplifying and minimizing the footprint of critical constraints; and

facilitate and steward team charters with domain-appropriate methods across project and product management.

The noun project can be defined as “an individual or collaborative enterprise that is carefully planned to achieve a particular aim.” A project starts with a known set of outputs—a scope. That scope might be something like “build a new airport capable of supporting 1,500 flights per day” or “release for scale manufacturing a device capable of supporting [company's] requirements for an AI-enabled voice assistant.” Project managers (PrMs) are successful to the extent that they can accommodate their stakeholders' needs with regard to cost and timing, while fulfilling the expected scope by completing a deliverable. Part of doing that is minimizing waste and optimizing against constraints, but another part is facilitating intentional decisions about timing versus cost when things don't go according to plan. The center of gravity for a project is often a “critical path,” a long sequence of dependent executions that determines a project's timeline and overall duration (see Figure 1). A PrM's job often requires responding to circumstances and deciding on the right people, processes, and resources to minimize delays along the critical path, especially when time is limited.

detail.abstract:
This case explores Annapurna Finance Pvt. Ltd. (AFPL) and its collaboration with Accion International and Mastercard through the Mastercard-Accion Partnership (MAP) to advance digital financial inclusion in India. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the partners developed the Just in Time (JIT) emergency loan—a small, flexible, and fully digital credit line designed to help low-income borrowers access funds instantly during emergencies. As demand for the JIT loan plateaus in the post-pandemic era, Accion's senior director of digital strategy Debdoot Banerjee must assess how to adapt the product for long-term impact.The case is intended for courses in inclusive finance, digital transformation, and social impact strategy. It allows students to explore themes of financial inclusion, innovation in microfinance, and cross-sector partnerships between global corporations and local financial institutions. Instructors can use the case to analyze the economics and design of digital loan products, the challenges of reaching underserved populations, and the tension between scalability and sustainability in impact finance.

Excerpt

Annapurna Finance: Just in Time

Accion International's (Accion's) senior director of digital strategy and transformation, Debdoot Banerjee, was always interested in the latest data on the Just in Time (JIT) emergency loan from Annapurna Finance Pvt. Ltd. (AFPL). It was May 2023, and after a quick rise in demand in late 2021 and 2022, the number of JIT loan requests was plateauing. There were some seasonal upticks in demand around the start of school and festival season. However, with the worst of the COVID-19 pandemic in the past, fewer clients were drawing on the loan—despite clearly valuing the AFPL membership benefit of having access to the product at any time. The loan had supported more than 200,000 customers since its launch, and AFPL was keen to explore whether it could be useful to clients as more than a pandemic emergency tool. The JIT loan was the result of over two years of effort combining Accion's technological expertise in microfinance innovation, Mastercard Incorporated's (Mastercard's) expertise in digital payments, and AFPL's ability to bring underserved Indians into the digital economy.

Accion

UC Berkeley Law student Joe Blatchford founded Accion in 1961 to conduct hands-on development projects in South America. As one early leader stated, Accion's mission was “not to give people alms, but to give them confidence in their own ability.” The organization's first projects were in Venezuela, where workers typically gained trust with poor communities by organizing sports leagues. After listening to the community's needs, workers led groups of locals in neighborhood improvement projects such as digging sewers and installing sidewalks. Over time, local labor and organizers replaced Accion workers. “That's what we want to do—work ourselves out of a job,” said Blatchford. Over the 1960s, Accion expanded to Brazil and Colombia.

In 1973, Accion launched a new credit product in Recife, Brazil, through a subsidiary, UNO, that provided small individual loans to “microenterprises” (a term coined by UNO) at interest rates typically only available for large commercial borrowers. To the amazement of its funders, the program faced no losses from non-repayment in its first years. “This was the first time any of these people had any of these people had any outside credit whatsoever, and it had a dramatic effect. The problem was that once we reached 100 people, we wanted to reach 500,” said Bruce Tippett, the organizer of the Recife UNO program. After launching a second successful program in Salvador, Brazil, Accion began to concentrate on providing microcredit. Throughout the 1980s, Accion opened microfinance programs in 14 Latin American countries.

Between 1990 and 2020, Accion deepened its efforts in Latin America and launched microfinance programs in the United States, sub-Saharan Africa, and Asia. During this period, the organization developed pioneering new financial-inclusion programs such as BancoSol in Bolivia, the first private commercial bank for poor people. In 2003, Accion began attracting investment from private banks through Accion Investments in Microfinance, the first global equity fund for microfinance. In 2008, Accion launched the Center for Financial Inclusion, a think tank that researched ways to make the financial system more inclusive and responsible. In 2012, Accion created Accion Venture Lab, a seed-stage impact-investment initiative focused on inclusive fintech. This was complemented in 2015 by the launch of the Accion Frontier Inclusion Fund, managed by Quona Capital. The first global fintech fund, the Accion Frontier Inclusion Fund further leveraged capital markets to take new innovations to scale. In May 2024, Accion announced the $152.5 million Accion Digital Transformation Fund to deploy strategic capital to support microfinance institutions and finance companies in connecting underserved clients to the digital economy. As Iain Brougham, Accion's vice president of digital strategy and transformation, explained, “We use philanthropy and Accion's balance sheet to test the most innovative solutions. We learn what's working through research and engagement, leveraging the capital markets to scale the most effective innovations and business models, replicating them in different markets to deliver systems-level change for millions of underserved people globally.” Since its founding, Accion helped to build 285 financial service providers across 76 countries, reaching 478 million people and trailblazing new pathways for including underserved populations in the financial system.

detail.title: Parental Separations: Developments, Causes and Consequences
detail.abstract: Parental separation is a common event in childhood, yet the developments and consequences for children remain poorly understood. We use novel data on parental colocation in Sweden to study parental separations for cohorts born from the 1950s until the 2000s. While high-SES families are as stable today as in the 1960s, the stability of low-SES households has markedly decreased. We also document pronounced geographical polarisation, with changes that are consistent with the declining marriage market value of men in traditionally manufacturing areas. Capturing all types of parental separation is critical, as restricting attention to divorce substantially underestimates the SES gradient and changes over time. We find limited effects of parental separation events on standardized test scores, but substantial effects on teacher-assigned grades, and consequently, on the probability of enrolling in the academic high school track.

detail.abstract: Strategic energy system planning is crucial for achieving sustainable and resilient energy systems. This process relies on comprehensive analyses that integrate economic, technological, environmental, and social factors to ensure reliable system development. Mathematical optimization forms the foundation of such planning, with Energy System Optimization Models (ESOMs) widely used for designing transition strategies.Within ESOMs, Capacity Expansion Models (CEMs) determine the cost-optimal mix of generation, storage, and transmission infrastructure to meet future energy demands while considering renewable integration, storage deployment, and grid expansion. detail.title: When the People Cry Out: A Community Council Model Amidst the Illusion of Popular Representation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual framework for a Community Council as an alternative legislative model in Indonesia, emphasizing community-based representation over political party-based representation. The study aims to expand theoretical understanding of functional representation, vote proportionality, and legislative governance. The proposed model places members through internal community mechanisms and assigns vote weights based on policy impact, allowing the most affected communities to wield greater influence in decision-making. This approach challenges the traditional assumption that legislative legitimacy can only be obtained through political parties or national elections, and offers a new mechanism to improve public policy responsiveness and accountability. The community-based legislative model has practical implications for public administration and policy, including increased accountability, transparency, and policy relevance, while reducing vote-buying and inefficient budget allocation. Theoretically, the framework paves the way for empirical research, simulations, development of policy impact indicators, and exploration of potential future adoption of innovative legislative models.

title: Analytics for On-Demand Food Delivery: A Hurwicz Satisficing Perspective
affiliations: , University of Sydney Business School and Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies

detail.title: Analytics for On-Demand Food Delivery: A Hurwicz Satisficing Perspective
detail.abstract: Problem definition: We study an on-demand food delivery (OFD) platform that dynamically coordinates customers, restaurants, and couriers under uncertainty to achieve multiple operational objectives, such as minimizing delivery delays and expirations, reducing costs, and enhancing value creation. The platform assigns orders and recommends courier relocations to balance supply and demand across spatial and temporal dimensions. This coordination is complicated by multiple sources of uncertainty-such as customer and courier arrivals, delivery times, and heterogeneous courier behaviors-whose underlying distributions are ambiguous and difficult to estimate reliably. Methodology/results: To address these challenges, we propose a Hurwicz satisficing optimization (HSO) framework for decision-making under uncertainty that integrates multiple objectives with forwardlooking considerations. The framework features the Hurwicz certainty equivalent (HCE) to balance optimism and pessimism in decision-makers' attitudes toward ambiguity, relaxing the fully pessimistic assumption inherent in robust optimization. To enhance robustness, we incorporate a satisficing mechanism that determines the minimal optimism level required to meet performance targets, while maintaining computational tractability through the analytical properties of the HCE. The HSO model is implemented for OFD operations using a rolling-horizon mixed-integer program, evaluated through both simulation and a real-world case study based on Meituan data. Implications: Compared with benchmark models, the HSO model consistently achieves balanced and robust performance across multiple operational metrics under different scenarios, highlighting the value of combining robust satisficing and the Hurwicz criterion in addressing uncertainty. The proposed framework advances the literature by providing a flexible, tractable, and practically implementable approach for large-scale OFD platforms, with broad applicability to other problem settings for decision-making under ambiguity.

title: Revolutionizing Transportation: The Future of High-Speed Rail Networks

detail.title: Revolutionizing Transportation: The Future of High-Speed Rail Networks
detail.abstract:
High-speed rail (HSR) networks are at the forefront of revolutionizing transportation by providing a fast, efficient, and sustainable alternative to traditional modes of travel. This paper explores the transformative potential of HSR, examining its impact on economic development, environmental sustainability, and urban planning. By analyzing successful case studies from around the world, we highlight the benefits of HSR in reducing travel times, creating jobs, and boosting local economies.
Despite its advantages, the implementation of HSR faces challenges such as financial constraints, regulatory hurdles, and social impacts on communities. Addressing these issues is crucial for achieving widespread public support and successful integration into existing transportation systems. Looking ahead, advancements in technology and growing awareness of
environmental concerns position HSR as a key player in future transportation solutions. This paper emphasizes the need for strategic planning and innovative approaches to ensure that HSR networks not only enhance mobility but also contribute to sustainable development and resilient urban environments. Ultimately, the future of high-speed rail holds the promise of reshaping how we connect, travel, and interact within and between cities.

title: Centralized Student Choice and Assignment Systems in China's Mandatory Education

detail.title: Centralized Student Choice and Assignment Systems in China's Mandatory Education
detail.abstract: The adoption of Centralized Student Choice and Assignment Systems (CCAS) has been on the rise worldwide. From 2003 to 2022, major Chinese cities gradually established CCAS in primary and secondary school admissions. I assemble the first dataset that documents the presence and attributes of CCAS for all 134 cities whose populations exceeded one million each. I provide descriptive evidence on the adoption patterns and heterogeneity in implementation details. I then estimate a diffusion model to investigate determinants of CCAS adoption. Results suggest city population and male average education correlate with earlier adoption, with caveats of small sample size and the difficulty in identifying peer effects. The coverage and heterogeneity of CCAS warrant more research on their optimal local forms and welfare implications.

detail.abstract: The Long-Wave Innovation & Shock Model (LWISM) integrates macroeconomic cycles, investment dynamics, and innovation processes under natural and deliberate shocks. The model formalizes how excess liquidity and real interest rates drive productive investment, which probabilistically generates innovation (Innovation Activation Probability, IAP), influencing long-term economic growth. The model contributes a novel probabilistic framework for understanding innovation-driven growth under complex shocks and provides a practical tool for forecasting, policy analysis, and strategic planning.

detail.abstract: Global finance no longer suffers from a shortage of liquidity but from a shortage of coordination. Regulatory fragmentation, technological divergence, and geopolitical tension have produced abundant yet immobilized capital. Sovereign payment systems, private networks, and decentralized ledgers each secure value within their own jurisdictions, but their isolation creates friction in motion. This paper examines how a Neutral Settlement Layer (NSL) can restore liquidity mobility by providing a lawful and interoperable framework for atomic settlement. The NSL is not a new monetary order but a connective architecture through which sovereign, institutional, and decentralized systems exchange value with equal assurance of completion. Deterministic consensus mechanisms, illustrated by the XRP Ledger, demonstrate the technical conditions under which such assurance can exist, while prudential standards, including the PFMI, Basel III, and ISO 20022, provide its legal and regulatory foundation. Reframing trust as a product of coordination rather than control, the paper argues that financial evolution will integrate rather than replace existing infrastructures, advancing a global framework in which confidence and liquidity operate as a single system of shared finality.

title: Impact of Global Geopolitical Risk on Equity Market Returns in South Asia: Evidence from a Structural VAR Analysis

detail.title: Impact of Global Geopolitical Risk on Equity Market Returns in South Asia: Evidence from a Structural VAR Analysis
detail.abstract: This research looks to understand how global geopolitical risk impacts equity market returns in South Asia using country-specific Structural Vector Autoregressive (SVAR) models which control for global market uncertainty. The paper uses the Caldara-lacoviello Geopolitical Risk (GPR) Index to measure global geopolitical risk and the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) to measure global market uncertainty. The focus is on three countries in South Asia which are India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. For the analysis, the study takes monthly stock market index data for each country from January 2015 to December 2024. The SVAR models take a recursive identification structure. It is assumed that GPR can impact VIX, but that VIX can not impact GPR and that both the GPR and the VIX can impact the equity returns but not vice versa. The results show that the impact of GPR shocks on the returns in these stock markets is mostly insignificant. This suggests that the GPR shocks are transmitted mostly through global market uncertainty as the model controls for global market uncertainty when studying the impact of GPR shocks. Global market uncertainty shocks on the other hand, have a strong and significant negative impact on stock market returns. The results are similar for all three countries. However, in the case of Bangladesh, the results are not statistically significant and less meaningful. This could be due to the Bangladesh stock market being less interconnected with the rest of the world compared to India and Pakistan.

title: Manning the Barricades: How Mann Construction Redefines IRS Rulemaking and Compliance Power
affiliations: University of Akron - The George W. Daverio School of Accountancy

detail.title: Manning the Barricades: How Mann Construction Redefines IRS Rulemaking and Compliance Power

keywords: Corner Post v. Board of Governors

detail.abstract:
For decades, the IRS has wielded sub-regulatory guidance as a cornerstone of tax enforcement, imposing compliance obligations through notices, revenue rulings, and revenue procedures without undergoing the notice-and-comment process required by the Administrative Procedure Act. Courts largely deferred to this approach, accepting the agency’s position that tax administration is too complex and urgent to be constrained by traditional rulemaking. That period is now ending.

Mann Construction, Inc. v. United States exposed the vulnerability of IRS informal rulemaking, holding that the agency cannot impose substantive obligations without adhering to procedural safeguards. The significance of this ruling has only grown in the wake of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, where the Supreme Court rejected Chevron deference and required courts to interpret statutes independently rather than relying on agency interpretations. These decisions have fundamentally reshaped the balance of power between agencies and courts, leaving the IRS in a precarious position. As judicial skepticism mounts, a core question arises: can tax administration function effectively if every enforcement tool must go through the slow and resource-intensive formal rulemaking process?

This Article argues that Mann Construction is not merely about one IRS notice but a broader judicial shift that threatens the agency’s long-standing enforcement framework. The increasing use of the Administrative Procedure Act challenges has led to forum shopping, regional inconsistencies, and growing uncertainty in tax compliance. The IRS now faces a choice. It can align its rulemaking process with judicial expectations, relying more on formal Treasury regulations, or it can seek congressional intervention to codify key enforcement tools and insulate them from procedural challenges. The judiciary must also confront the unintended consequences of this shift, as tax administration risks becoming fragmented across circuits, undermining the uniformity of federal tax law.

The future of tax enforcement is at an inflection point. Without a coordinated response, the IRS will continue to face escalating legal challenges that weaken its ability to regulate effectively. The question is no longer whether the agency must adapt but whether it can do so quickly enough to prevent its authority from eroding beyond repair.

title: AI: The Community Approach. It's All About the People
affiliations: and Cardiff University

detail.title: AI: The Community Approach. It's All About the People
detail.abstract: How a simple roadmap for navigating AI in an organisation that delivers better business outcomes and digital agility. No one knows everything about AI and that's exactly why we need each other. That's the foundational insight behind Cardiff University's approach to AI adoption, one that's delivering measurable results and offering a blueprint for other organisations. Instead of pretending to have all the answers, they created a space for honest conversations about what's working, what isn't, and what they're learning along the way. Our roadmap is simple: Mindset → Cultivate a growth mindset. Stay curious and take a balanced view. AI isn't perfect, but could it be useful? Try responsible AI approaches. Let's not lose critical skills and protect our data. This foundational shift moves organisations from binary thinking about AI to nuanced evaluation of its role, embracing learning over knowing. Conversations → Share what worked well and what didn't. Honest conversations are everything. These aren't formal presentations but real dialogue about successes, failures, and lessons learned. Staff need safe spaces to admit confusion and seek help.

title: Sukavichinomics and the Structural Reform of Agricultural and Fisheries Debt in Thailand
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Sukavichinomics and the Structural Reform of Agricultural and Fisheries Debt in Thailand
detail.abstract: This article examines the development of Thailand's debt restructuring measures for farmers and fisherfolk initiated in 1997, through the lens of Sukavichinomics-a philosophy grounded in people-centered development, accountable policy design, and multi-sectoral integration. Contrary to popular belief that debt moratorium programs emerged from populist governments post-2001, this study demonstrates that such measures were rooted in a structural policy framework established prior to that period. Employing a narrative timeline analysis based on primary sources-including publications in the Royal Gazette and official regulations from the Office of the Prime Minister-the study traces the formalization of these measures. On 29 March 1997, the Thai Cabinet approved the Regulation of the Prime Minister's Office on the Farmers Assistance Fund (No. 2) and appointed Deputy Prime Minister His Excellency Mr. Sukavich Rangsitpol as Chair of the National Policy Committee on Farmers' Debt. The regulation was officially promulgated in the Royal Gazette on 3 April 1997, alongside the formation of a monitoring and evaluation committee to ensure transparency, legal legitimacy, and oversight. Subsequently, on 26 August 1997, Regulation No. 3 was enacted to extend debt restructuring protections to fisherfolk, reflecting a deliberate policy commitment to inclusive development and the principle of "leaving no one behind." The findings underscore that the 1997 debt restructuring initiative was not a populist measure, but rather a systematic structural reform integrating legal frameworks, targeted institutional mechanisms, and robust monitoring protocols. As such, it represents a model of sustainable public policy that is both legally grounded and ethically accountable, offering a compelling counterpoint to short-term, politically driven policy interventions.
