detail.abstract: Pune, a city with rich history-ranging from its origin as a Maratha military center to role as a IT/ITES hub-has witnessed a rapid urbanization. The implementation of the Unified Development Control and Promotion Regulations (UDCPR) in 2020 has reignited lot of debates concerning environmental sustainability, optimal land use and social equity. This study aims to look at the multifaceted implications of Floor Space Index (FSI) policy in Pune through a semi-structured interview of key stakeholders. To understand the implications, this study employs purposive sampling of various stakeholders such as urban activists, environmentalists, builders and subject matter experts gathering the first-hand information and the lived experience of policy implementation. Thematic analysis of the interviews suggests five key factors of the FSI debate (1) an engineering-led paradigm that hindered collaborative decision making across municipal bodies. (2) contextual use of FSI, debates on vertical and horizontal growth model and importance of carrying-capacity of local infrastructure. (3) need for clear vision and roadmap for a city development (4) importance of sustainability and livability (5) policy as a key driver of urban forms where political will and accountability mechanisms determine implementation efficacy. Findings of this study underline that while increased FSI can ensure housing supply and economic returns, it risks increasing congestion, straining public infrastructure and diminishing ecological assets, if infrastructural investments and governance reforms are not adequate. Based on stakeholder recommendations, following policy interventions can be carried out: conducting carryingcapacity assessments prior FSI revisions; exploring the possibility of satellite towns; promoting interdisciplinary decision making; articulating long term vision documents and abiding by it; enforcing strict rules to preserve cultural and environmental aspects.

title: Flow Acceleration and the IHACC Model: Human-AI Co-Creation in Epistemology

detail.title: Flow Acceleration and the IHACC Model: Human-AI Co-Creation in Epistemology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Iterative Human-AI Co-Creation (IHACC) model as a conceptual framework for knowledge production in the age of generative AI. IHACC describes a recursive process in which human agents, AI systems and feedback loops jointly generate, test and refine ideas. At its core is "flow acceleration": the AI-mediated compression of the classical data-information-knowledge-wisdom progression into rapid human-AI interaction cycles, while leaving humans in charge of epistemic goals, standards and responsibility. Drawing on actor-network perspectives and the notion of the infosphere, IHACC treats knowledge not as a static product but as an emergent property of socio-technical processes, even as it acknowledges Heideggerian concerns about reduction of the world to mere resource. The model synthesizes empirical findings on productivity gains and error risks from large language models, interpreting them as evidence of reconfigured epistemic agency and temporality rather than simple efficiency effects. The paper argues that IHACC is a candidate paradigm shift in epistemology because it relocates the locus of "knowing" into governed human-AI systems and opens new possibilities for epistemic justice, while also posing normative questions about dependence, opacity and control in accelerated knowledge infrastructures. We position IHACC as a base model for accelerated human-AI inquiry and specify propositions that invite direct testing.

title: Development of an Automated Web Application for Efficient Web Scraping: Design and Implementation
affiliations: Adamas University, Adamas University, Adamas University, Adamas University and

detail.title: Development of an Automated Web Application for Efficient Web Scraping: Design and Implementation
detail.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a user-friendly, automated web application that simplifies and optimizes the web scraping process for non-technical users. The application breaks down the complex task of web scraping into three main stages: fetching, extraction, and execution. In the fetching stage, the application accesses target websites using the HTTP protocol, leveraging the requests library to retrieve HTML content. The extraction stage utilizes powerful parsing libraries like BeautifulSoup and regular expressions to extract relevant data from the HTML. Finally, the execution stage structures the data into accessible formats, such as CSV, ensuring the scraped content is organized for easy use. To provide personalized and secure experiences, the application includes user registration and login functionalities, supported by MongoDB, which stores user data and scraping history. Deployed using the Flask framework, the tool offers a scalable, robust environment for web scraping. Users can easily input website URLs, define data extraction parameters, and download the data in a simplified format, without needing technical expertise. This automated tool not only enhances the efficiency of web scraping but also democratizes access to data extraction by empowering users of all technical levels to gather and manage data tailored to their needs. The methodology detailed in this paper represents a significant advancement in making web scraping tools accessible, efficient, and easy to use for a broader audience.

title: Orchestrated Intelligence: Rethinking Knowledge Work in the Age of AI

detail.title: Orchestrated Intelligence: Rethinking Knowledge Work in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of publicly accessible generative AI tools has triggered widespread debate on automation and job displacement. Yet a more immediate and underexplored transformation lies in how these tools reconfigure the capacity of individual professionals. This paper introduces the concept of Orchestrated Intelligence: a human-led, workflow-based approach that leverages AI not for substitution, but for amplification. Grounded in the Iterative Human-AI Co-Creation (IHACC) model (Simpson, 2025), the study employs a structured simulation in which a single user produced the equivalent output of a research and communication team, including economic modeling, multilingual reporting, and stakeholder-specific dissemination, within three hours using only public AI systems. Findings show time compression, multi-format output, and narrative coherence under explicit orchestration. We define the method, report a single-session case with quantified metrics, and discuss implications for training, institutional design, and authorship. Materials transparency is provided via a brief orchestration manifest and checklist available on request.

title: The Experience of Implementing Digital Innovations in the U.S. Startup Ecosystem and the Opportunities for Application in Uzbekistan
affiliations: Samarkand Institute of Economics and Service, Master. Uzbekistan. and Samarkand Institute of Economics and Service

detail.title: The Experience of Implementing Digital Innovations in the U.S. Startup Ecosystem and the Opportunities for Application in Uzbekistan
detail.abstract: This study explores the structural characteristics and operational mechanisms of the United States (U.S.) startup ecosystem in implementing digital innovations and evaluates their adaptability to Uzbekistan's emerging entrepreneurial environment. The research aims to analyze how the integration of technology, venture capital, and state policies in the U.S. has contributed to a sustainable innovation-driven economy and how these lessons can inform Uzbekistan's digital transformation strategy. A mixed-method comparative analysis was conducted between 2020 and 2024 using secondary data from global innovation indices, venture capital investment reports, and policy documents. Qualitative insights were drawn from academic literature and expert interviews available in public databases. The principal findings indicate that the U.S. startup ecosystem thrives due to its comprehensive infrastructurecharacterized by university-industry collaboration, venture funding mechanisms, and adaptive policy support. In contrast, Uzbekistan's ecosystem, though rapidly growing, remains constrained by limited financing, insufficient digital infrastructure, and weak university-industry integration. The research contributes to the understanding of how developing economies can localize global innovation practices through institutional reform and policy alignment. The implications of this study suggest that Uzbekistan can accelerate its digital innovation capacity by establishing venture funds, promoting entrepreneurial education, and incentivizing research commercialization. Socially, the findings underscore the potential for startups to enhance employment, sustainability, and digital inclusion. Despite the limitations associated with reliance on secondary data, this study provides a conceptual framework for policymakers, investors, and researchers to strengthen innovation ecosystems in transitional economies.

title: Public Knowledge Begins with Flux: Proposing a Spiral Model of Knowledge Evolution Beyond Peer Review
affiliations: Foods Support MORICA Co., Ltd.

detail.title: Public Knowledge Begins with Flux: Proposing a Spiral Model of Knowledge Evolution Beyond Peer Review
detail.abstract: This paper advances the proposition that the publicness of knowledge does not arise from stable foundations but rather from flux and instability. Traditional peer review has long served as a mechanism to secure the validity of academic claims and generate institutional authority. Yet, by imposing entry barriers, it has also constrained the public accessibility of knowledge. In contrast, the rise of preprint repositories and AI-driven knowledge generation exposes ideas to flux, enabling an accelerated and dynamic process of knowledge evolution. The contribution of this study is threefold: (1) it conceptualizes the dual function of peer review as both guaranteeing validity and generating authority; (2) it theorizes flux and instability as productive catalysts of intellectual "collisions" that refine knowledge; and (3) it introduces the model of Spiral Public Knowledge, framing knowledge development not as linear accumulation but as a spiral process that emerges through tension between stability and instability. The theoretical foundation integrates insights from philosophy of science (e.g., Kuhn's paradigm shifts), social theory (knowledge as socially constructed), and cross-cultural thought (pragmatism's experimentalism, Wang Yangming's unity of knowledge and action, and dialectical notions of sublation). Political democratization and biological evolution serve as analogies to illustrate how instability and order interact to drive progress. In conclusion, the paper argues that public knowledge evolves through the Aufhebung of authority and democratization, producing a spiral dynamic that transcends the dichotomy of peerreviewed versus non-peer-reviewed knowledge. This framework offers a new perspective on the future of knowledge in the era of Open Science and AI, highlighting flux not as a weakness but as the very condition of intellectual advancement.

title: Ethical Challenges and Privacy Concerns Associated with Big Data in the Hiring Process: A Mixed-Methods Study
affiliations: University of Rochester

detail.title: Ethical Challenges and Privacy Concerns Associated with Big Data in the Hiring Process: A Mixed-Methods Study
detail.abstract: Background: The advent of big data in recruitment processes has introduced more efficient, quicker, and scalable enhanced decision-making. Big data technologies enable recruiters to analyse vast amounts of candidate information, ostensibly improving the precision with which suitable candidates are identified. However, this technological advance also presents significant ethical challenges. Aims: This study aims to explore the ethical challenges and privacy concerns associated with the use of big data in recruitment processes, focusing on algorithmic bias, data privacy, and fairness in hiring practices. Methodology: The research employs a mixed-methods design, integrating qualitative interviews with HR professionals and quantitative data analysis to assess the implications of big data utilisation in recruitment. The study was conducted across various organisations, focusing on their recruitment practices, over six months. Qualitative interviews were conducted with HR professionals to gather insights on real-world experiences related to ethical challenges in recruitment. Additionally, a quantitative analysis of recruitment algorithms was performed to identify prevalent biases and their impact on hiring decisions, using statistical evidence to highlight significant findings. By triangulating these methods, the research robustly examined how big data applications alter recruitment landscapes, identifying ethical challenges and laying a foundation for potential solutions. Results: The findings reveal that algorithmic bias is a profound issue in recruitment, with 62% of surveyed HR professionals acknowledging its influence on hiring decisions. Moreover, significant concerns regarding data privacy emerged, with 75% of respondents indicating that handling sensitive candidate information lacks adequate safeguards, increasing the risk of unauthorised access. Addressing ethical concerns in big data recruitment necessitates the collaboration of multiple stakeholders, including HR

title: Liquidity Risk and Monetary Tightening: Evidence from Global Bond Markets
affiliations: World Bank Group Ecosystem

detail.title: Liquidity Risk and Monetary Tightening: Evidence from Global Bond Markets
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how monetary tightening affects market liquidity across global bond markets. It conceptualizes liquidity risk as a key transmission channel linking policy-rate changes to asset-price volatility and market depth. Using data from advanced and emerging markets, the study finds that a 100-basis-point increase in policy rates leads to a 15-25 percent widening in bid-ask spreads and a 10 percent drop in bond turnover, especially in emerging markets. These effects are driven by higher dealer funding costs and reduced risk appetite. The results suggest that liquidity risk amplifies monetary transmission and underscores the need for policies that maintain smooth market functioning during tightening cycles.

title: Stung into Action? Cyber Risk Management After a Breach
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London - School of Economics and Finance, Bayes Business School (formerly Cass), Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) and

detail.title: Stung into Action? Cyber Risk Management After a Breach
detail.abstract: We study how firms adapt their cybersecurity defenses following major cyber incidents. Combining multiple sources of incident disclosures with job posting data for U.S. listed firms between 2010 and 2022, we construct novel firm-level measures of cybersecurity labor demand, software use, and IT architectures. Incidents trigger substantial and persistent increases in cybersecurity hiring and adoption of advanced technologies. Affected firms leapfrog ahead of industry peers. Firms in the same industry and firms with similar IT systems also strengthen defenses. Among financial institutions, larger firms react more strongly, consistent with greater scrutiny and exposure to cyber risk.

title: The Direct and Local Spillover Effects of Subsidized Housing Investment: Evidence from a Tax Credit Lottery
affiliations: IBM Research, University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics and University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Direct and Local Spillover Effects of Subsidized Housing Investment: Evidence from a Tax Credit Lottery
detail.abstract: This paper examines the private response to tax incentives for residential investment as well as the nature and scope of housing externalities by exploiting the lottery structure of Missouri's Neighborhood Preservation Act (NPA). The NPA offers tax credits to homeowners and developers who improve or expand the owner-occupied housing stock in low-income areas. Taking advantage of the random assignment of NPA tax credits together with detailed property-level data, we find that the program increases construction activity over and above that which would have occurred in its absence. NPA-induced investments also translate into positive albeit imprecisely measured changes in property values. However, we find no evidence that NPA-subsidized investment affects neighbors' investment behavior or nearby property values. The results highlight the limits of housing improvement policies in spurring broad-based neighborhood change where it would not happen otherwise.

title: Scale-Dependent Returns and the Interest Rate

detail.title: Scale-Dependent Returns and the Interest Rate
detail.abstract: I revisit the empirical relationship between wealth and returns on wealth of U.S. households over the past 70 years. While recent studies suggest that returns on wealth increase with wealth and that the richest households earn the highest returns, I show that this pattern is specific to post-1980. Before 1980, returns declined at the top 10 percentiles of the wealth distribution, and the bottom 90 percentiles had higher returns than the top 10 percent. I attribute this reversal to differences in households' exposure to interest rate risk. Because wealthier households tend to hold longer-duration assets, such as stocks and private businesses, changes in real interest rates affect their portfolios more strongly. When real rates rose, as they did before 1980, the top 10 percentiles households experienced lower returns, whereas falling real rates after 1980 boosted their returns. To explain why wealthier households hold longer-duration assets, I develop a model in which households select portfolio duration to hedge their income risk. Since richer households' income correlates more with short-term interest rates, they optimally choose a longer-duration (countercyclical) to hedge this exposure.

detail.abstract: The mandate of art.21 TEU attributes a central role to the EU's constitutional values as guiding principles for external action. This marks an important aspect of "external constitutional law" and puts the EU into the role of an "exporter" of values. Yet, the systematic conceptualization and operationalization of these values remain underdeveloped. A gap between rhetoric and practice undermines the EU's coherence and effectiveness in promoting its values abroad. The dichotomy in the EU's external competences complicates a consistent development of values and legal standards. For consistency and as a matter of identity of the Union, the substance of values by which the EU is guided externally should be the same as in the internal dimension. Recent strategies aimed at enhancing value-based external action suffer from inconsistencies in their implementation. Yet, consistency is both a legal obligation and a practical necessity for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU external action. Both could be increased by learning from the lessons of the internal dimension of value protection.

title: Luck as a Mixed Blessing
affiliations: McDonough School of Business, University of Georgia - Terry College of Business - Department of Finance, Vanderbilt University - Finance Department and Ohio State University (OSU)

detail.title: Luck as a Mixed Blessing
detail.abstract: We study two forms of early-career luck, placement luck (the initial pairing of worker and firm) and performance luck (early productivity shocks), in a unified framework that characterizes both their benefits and costs for workers' career outcomes. Estimating the model using granular career and deal-flow data for investment bankers, we find results partly consistent with prior evidence of positive long-run effects. Our results, however, also reveal new mechanisms and novel implications. Placement luck benefits high-ability workers by placing them in productive pairs early, yet it can be a mixed blessing for low-ability workers, whose poor match quality and elevated separation risk erode long-run gains. Performance luck boosts learning and human-capital growth in good matches, but it distorts beliefs and delays necessary job transitions in poor ones, producing long-run setbacks. The framework is applicable to other high-skill professions, where varying frictions and market structures may yield different impacts of early-career luck.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how monetary policy affects corporate lending through its impact on household balance sheets, bridging the gap between the cash flow and bank lending channels. When policy rates rise, households with variable-rate debt face higher monthly payments, prompting early mortgage repayments, particularly among high-income borrowers. Exploiting the monetary tightening between July 2022 and September 2023 as a policy experiment, we show that banks that are more exposed to variable-rate mortgages granted to higher-income households increase their supply of corporate credit, especially to micro and small firms. However, no variation is observed in the balance of household credit or in other investment items on the banks’ balance sheets. Indeed, banks facing higher liquidity constraints tend to extend more corporate credit as their exposure to early redemptions increases. Our findings provide new evidence on how household financial constraints shape monetary policy transmission, offering novel insights into the interplay between household debt dynamics and corporate credit allocation.

title: Bankruptcy as Political Resistance

detail.title: Bankruptcy as Political Resistance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Indiana Legal Studies Research Paper No. 568
publicationDetails.journalName: Indiana University Maurer School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Litigation against President Trump for withholding federal funds from cities in his “war on woke” has taken place either in Article III courts under the Administrative Procedure Act or in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act. However, there is a third place to resolve these disputes and allocate who bears the consequences of Presidential action that no one has discussed…bankruptcy courts. Federal grants make up about 1/3rd of the average city’s budget, and the President could render a city insolvent by swiftly cutting off a city’s federal grants before a city could seek to enjoin such an action through a process scholars call “appropriations presidentialism”. If the President did so, then the thousands of workers, vendors, and creditors that rely on those funds as a source of payment would most likely file suit against these cities within weeks to seek payment. In other words, the city’s financial position would be like an “ice cube” rapidly melting away in the hot summer sun.

This Essay argues that cities facing “governance by extortion” can use the filing of bankruptcy as an act of political resistance to manage a city’s presidentially induced bankruptcy. In many ways, bankruptcy courts are in a better position than Title III courts to provide relief in this case. Bankruptcy courts have the legal and equitable tools that Art. III courts lack and that indebted cities will need to handle creditor coordination problems that are likely to occur when federal grant funds run out. This Essay’s exploration of bankruptcy’s relationship with administrative law expands conversations about the institutional capacity of the judicial system to manage the effects of appropriations presidentialism. Additionally, this Essay situates bankruptcy as a device for coordinating political resistance of governance by extortion.

title: When Capital Becomes Curse: The Conditional Impact of Chinese Investment in Fragile States

detail.title: When Capital Becomes Curse: The Conditional Impact of Chinese Investment in Fragile States

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the economic efficacy of Chinese development finance depends critically on recipient-region security conditions. Using a novel province-year panel dataset (2010-2020) covering the Democratic Republic of Congo's 26 provinces, we employ a robust panel fixed effects regression model with interaction terms to identify the causal impact of Chinese investment flows on provincial GDP per capita. The analysis reveals a stark conditional asymmetry: while Chinese investment generates significant positive returns in stable provinces (β 1 = +1.52, p < 0.01)-with each additional million USD associated with a 1.52 increase in GDP per capita-this effect is completely reversed in conflict-prone provinces. The total marginal effect in highconflict eastern regions (North Kivu, South Kivu, Ituri, Tanganyika) is negative and statistically significant (calculated as β 1 + β 2 =-0.43, p < 0.05), indicating that identical capital inflows paradoxically correlate with economic decline rather than growth. Analysis of comparison group trends supports the causal interpretation. These findings demonstrate a severe "Fragility Penalty" where institutional weakness and chronic conflict transform development finance from a growth accelerator into a destabilizing force. The results challenge the "Chinese Exception Hypothesis" and reveal that resourcebacked infrastructure investment, absent conflict-sensitive safeguards and institutional capacity, may exacerbate rather than alleviate economic stagnation in fragile states.

title: The Procyclical Disinvestment of Productive Non-Market Time (PNMT): A Causal Mechanism for Recessionary Scarring and Widening Inequality

detail.title: The Procyclical Disinvestment of Productive Non-Market Time (PNMT): A Causal Mechanism for Recessionary Scarring and Widening Inequality

detail.abstract: This paper investigates a behavioral mechanism for recessionary scarring: procyclical disinvestment in Productive Non-Market Time (PNMT). We define PNMT as self-directed human capital investment, such as skill acquisition and specialized job search. Using ATUS-CPS data (2004-2016), we employ a robust staggered differencein-differences design to identify the causal impact of macroeconomic shocks on this behavior. The analysis shows that a 1 percentage point increase in the state-level unemployment rate causes a 7.47-minute decrease (p<0.01) in average daily PNMT. This finding contradicts the classical substitution hypothesis, suggesting that behavioral discouragement and binding liquidity constraints dominate. Furthermore, this procyclical disinvestment is significantly larger for non-college workers (8.24 minutes) (p<0.05) than for college-educated workers (6.67 minutes) (p<0.05). This identifies a critical, self-reinforcing channel for inequality. These findings reveal that recessions force workers, particularly the most vulnerable, to disinvest in human capital maintenance at the precise moment that skill depreciation poses the greatest threat, thereby providing a direct behavioral explanation for persistent recessionary scarring.

detail.abstract: The study examines methodologies for quantitatively analyzing the impact of global supply chain fragmentation and applies these approaches to scenarios involving critical minerals. It identifies two primary analytical approaches: microeconomic and macroeconomic. Microeconomic methods provide detailed insights at the item or firm level but face challenges due to limited access to specific supply chain data. Macroeconomic methods, while suitable for industry- or national-level analysis, often rely on unrealistic assumptions when applied to item-level fragmentation. Despite the significant macroeconomic effects of disruptions in critical supply chains, existing item-level analysis techniques struggle to capture these impacts accurately. For instance, efforts to link item-level analysis with GDP using linear programming or inoperability input-output analysis often encounter limitations due to rigid assumptions about input-output structures. detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of bilateral exchange with bounded monetary transferability. Agents hold heterogeneous goods and engage in direct swaps, with optional cash top-ups that bridge valuation gaps. Valuations are expressed in a common numeraire (USD) to anchor preferences, but transfers are capped to preserve the identity of barter. This structure defines a regime of hybrid barter that lies between nontransferable and fully transferable utility. We show that bounded transfers expand the feasible set of trades and weakly improve welfare relative to pure barter when transfer frictions are small. The model generalizes the transferable-utility assignment game of Shapley and Shubik (1971) by imposing bounded transferability, creating a continuum between barter and full monetary exchange. It connects search-and-matching theory with assignment games, offering a tractable framework for analyzing decentralized exchange under costly liquidity.

title: The Effect of Social Trust on Economic Growth With Emphasis on the Case of Iran

detail.title: The Effect of Social Trust on Economic Growth With Emphasis on the Case of Iran
detail.abstract: Today, most social and economic scientists have accepted the important role of extra-economic factors such as social trust in the process of economic development of societies. According to them, public trust is not only effective by creating cooperation and coordination between individuals and groups and reducing the costs of production, distribution and exchange in the economic system, but also in many other ways on economic growth. This article, while examining the ways of influencing social trust on economic development, tries to provide a conceptual framework and a practical definition of social trust and its adaptation to the conditions of growth in today's Iranian society. In this research, the method of applying the model of social trust to the last four decades of Iranian society and several approaches have been used for the model of the mechanism of the effect of social trust on economic growth. The article concludes: "Responsibility, efficient management, increasing business transactions, reducing possible risks in transactions, increasing domestic and foreign investment, reducing investment costs, creating welfare states" among the factors. They are an effective mediator in the mechanism of social trust and economic growth.

title: The East Asian Emotional Economy Model (EAEEM): How Confucian-Buddhist Scripts Convert Love into Obligation and Filiality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Inspired by Gabor Maté's The Wisdom of Trauma, this paper begins with the idea that trauma disconnects individuals from their authentic selves. In Western psychology, trauma is usually associated with visible causes such as violence, addiction, or isolation. In many East Asian countries, people often find it difficult to articulate the origins of their distress, which delays seeking help and hampers healing. This study examines the phenomenon of "emotional aphasia" in East Asia and investigates its cultural and structural roots. This article employs accounting and economic terminology to model the logic of the East Asian emotional system, specifically the East Asian Emotional Economy Model (EAEEM). The model indicates that emotions have been economically managed at both social and family levels in East Asia, transforming En (obligation) and Ai (affection) into quantifiable emotional assets and expenses. It aims to investigate the roots of this intergenerational trauma through the cultural lens of Confucian-Buddhist traditions and the literary perspective of inherited poems and personal anecdotes. Two sub-models operationalise the family-level dynamics: the Emotional ROI Model and the Emotional Ledger Theory (ELT). Finally, the paper proposes three intervention models. Emotional Reprogramming through Reflective Literacy (ER-RL) helps people distinguish between self-generated emotion and duty-driven scripts. Reflective Animal Intervention (RAI) offers an embodied route to relearn care beyond moral coercion. The Inner Fire Reignition Plan supports individuals in transforming invisibility into agency through micro-actions of selfrecognition. The paper concludes with testable propositions and discusses implications for emotional literacy and relational healing in East Asian contexts.

title: The Strength of Weak Ties in Commons Governance: Cross-Community Networks and the Enforcement of Environmental Rules
affiliations: College of Charleston

detail.title: The Strength of Weak Ties in Commons Governance: Cross-Community Networks and the Enforcement of Environmental Rules
detail.abstract: A rich literature on common-pool resources (CPRs) demonstrates that strong intra-community ties-the dense bonds of kinship, friendship, and frequent interaction-underpin effective local governance by fostering trust, reciprocity, and robust monitoring. This understanding has spawned a dominant policy paradigm of "community fortification." However, many critical CPRs, such as fisheries, span multiple communities, creating an "inter-community domain" where the resource system is cross-boundary, while governance remains rooted in localized, intra-community dynamics. This disconnect explains why conventional community-based institutions often falter, as seen with East Africa's Beach Management Units (BMUs). Although legally mandated for inclusivity, BMUs remained anchored in localized structures and failed to enforce rules across communities, leaving cross-community overfishing unchecked. This article argues that governing these shared resources requires a different social architecture, where weak ties-Mark Granovetter's conceptualization of infrequent, instrumental bridges between social groups-become paramount. Analyzing the case of militarized fisheries governance on Buvuma Island, I reveal a critical mechanism: A coalition of affluent fishermen leveraged pre-existing, cross-community weak ties, formed through seasonal migration, to construct an inter-community network. This network strategically partnered with state enforcers, providing localized intelligence and financial resources essential for coordinated enforcement. This led to a sharp reduction in illicit fishing and a significant fish stock recovery. My findings reconceptualize the "strength of weak ties" within commons theory, illustrating that effective environmental governance beyond the local scale is not merely an extension of community-based management, but a distinct process that depends on the strategic activation of cross-community bridges.

detail.abstract: Elasticity of factor substitution measures the degree (ease) at which one factor can be substituted by other when relative factor price changes, whereas factor augmenting technology refers to the adoption of a technology which is biased towards a particular factor (either capital or labour) irrespective of the change in relative factor prices (Youtopoulos et al .1976). The empirical estimation of elasticity of factor substitution has implications towards economic growth, distribution of income and many other macroeconomic variables. The far reaching impact of elasticity of factor substitution on steady-state conditions and other results like convergence has been widely studied (e.g. Turnovsky (2002), Grandville (1989), Klump and Grandville (2000), Klump and Preissler (2000), Miyagiwa and Papageorgiou (2003, 2007)). On empirical literature, estimated value of the elasticity of factor substitution found to vary substantially between crosssections to time-series data and is found to be sensitive on the methodology used to estimate elasticity. In the Indian context, Golder et al. (2013) found that the estimated value of the elasticity for 2digit manufacturing sector was less than unity for majority of the 2-digit industries between 1980-81 to 2006-07 and the technology adopted was mostly labour saving. In the literature there was large number of empirical papers which tried to estimate the elasticity of factor substitutions for Indian Manufacturing Sector (Banerjee (1971, 1973); Goldar (1986, 2012); Jha et.al (1991); Ahluwalia (1991); Virmani and Hasim (2009)).Using India KLEMS database we estimated the elasticity of factor substitution for Indian industries from 1980 to 2018.

detail.abstract: The swift evolution of digital technology has profoundly altered Human Resource Management (HRM) operations, redefining the methods by which organisations attract, cultivate, and retain talent. This article analyses the impact of essential technologies-such as automation, artificial intelligence, HR analytics, cloud-based HR systems, and digital communication tools-on fundamental HRM functions including recruitment, training, performance management, employee engagement, and strategic decision-making. The results show that technology makes things more efficient, accurate, and strategically aligned by making administrative duties easier, giving data-driven insights, and making employees' experiences better. However, using technology also comes with problems, such as worries about data protection, talent gaps, and the need for change management in organisations. The study finds that technology serves as a catalyst for the transformation of HRM from an administrative role to a strategic partner, highlighting the necessity of ongoing adaptation in a digitalised workplace.

title: AI and Worker Well-Being: Differential Impacts Across Generational Cohorts and Genders
affiliations: Faculty of Economics, Chulalongkorn University

detail.title: AI and Worker Well-Being: Differential Impacts Across Generational Cohorts and Genders
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between AI use and worker well-being outcomes-mental health, job enjoyment, and physical health and safety-using microdata from the OECD AI Surveys across seven countries. The results reveal that AI users are significantly more likely to report improvements across all three outcomes, with effects ranging from 8.9% to 21.3%. However, these benefits vary by generation and gender. Generation Y (1981-1996) shows the strongest gains across all dimensions, while Generation X (1965-1980) reports moderate improvements in mental health and job enjoyment. In contrast, Generation Z (1997-2012) benefits only in job enjoyment. As digital natives already familiar with technology, Gen Z workers may not receive additional gains in mental or physical health from AI, though they still experience increased enjoyment from using it. Baby Boomers (born before 1965) experience limited benefits, as they may not find these tools as engaging or useful. Women report stronger mental health gains, whereas men report greater improvements in physical health. These findings suggest that AI's workplace impact is uneven and shaped by demographic factors, career stage, and the nature of workers' roles.

title: Strategic Fragmentation: Endogenous Trade Retrenchment under Geopolitical Uncertainty

detail.title: Strategic Fragmentation: Endogenous Trade Retrenchment under Geopolitical Uncertainty
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical model of strategic fragmentation as an equilibrium response to belief-contingent enforcement risk. We embed a global-game framework where sovereign dyads receive private signals about geopolitical alignment and form posterior beliefs about contract enforceability. In equilibrium, fragmentation arises from a threshold strategy: dyads exit trade relationships when aggregate fragmentation exceeds a critical value. We establish the existence and uniqueness of this threshold equilibrium and demonstrate strategic complementarity in exit decisions. Comparative statics reveal that higher political alignment raises the exit threshold, while greater sunk costs and information noise lower it. The model exhibits hysteresis: re-entry requires more favorable conditions than exit, creating persistent fragmentation even after tensions subside. Welfare analysis shows that coordination failures generate significant efficiency losses. Calibrated counterfactuals suggest that neutral arbitration and transparency mandates substantially improve global welfare. Our framework explains why fragmentation concentrates in high-surplus, high-sunk-cost sectors and persists beyond geopolitical shocks, offering a rational expectations foundation for strategic decoupling.

detail.abstract: Cross-sectional data have proven to be increasingly useful for macroeconomic research. However, their use often leads to the 'missing intercept' problem in which aggregate general equilibrium effects and policy responses are absorbed into fixed effects. We present a statistical approach to jointly estimate aggregate and idiosyncratic effects within a panel framework, leveraging identification strategies coming from both cross-sectional or time-series settings. We then apply our methodology to study government spending multipliers (Nakamura and Steinsson, 2014) and wealth effects from stock returns (Chodorow-Reich et al., 2021).

detail.abstract: Debt financing is an integral component of the trade-off theory of optimal capital structure. This theory is one of the tools that can be integrated into the financial policy of a modern company to implement measures to maximize its value by managing the insolvency costs. The article revealed the nature of insolvency costs through their classification into explicit and implicit, and limitations associated with their quantitative assessment. The implicit cost of insolvency costs is inevitable, but effective management of their level is largely determined by the professional competencies of responsible employees. Achieving the target level of insolvency costs not only contributes to increasing company value for sustainable growth but also improves the economic climate by reducing the likelihood of bankruptcy.

title: Labor Supply Response to Windfall Gains

detail.title: Labor Supply Response to Windfall Gains

detail.abstract: Using a large survey of euro area consumers, we conduct an experiment in which respondents report how they would adjust their labor market participation, hours worked, and job search effort (if not employed) in response to randomly assigned windfall gain scenarios. Windfall gains reduce labor supply, but only when the gains are substantial. At the extensive margin, gains of €25,000 or less have no effects, while gains between €50,000 and €100,000 reduce the probability of working by 1.5 to 3.5 percentage points. At the intensive margin, small gains produce no impact, while gains above €50,000 lead to a reduction of approximately one hour of work per week. The effects among women and workers near retirement are stronger. The share of non-employed respondents who stop or reduce job search intensity declines by 1 percentage point for each €10,000 in windfall gain, with the strongest effects observed among older individuals receiving €100,000.

title: Economic Prosperity and Ethnic Identification: Evidence from Ethiopia

detail.title: Economic Prosperity and Ethnic Identification: Evidence from Ethiopia

detail.abstract: Since the early 1990s, Ethiopia has implemented an ethnic-based federal structure, with some pundits warning that this system fosters stronger allegiance to ethnic groups, thus risking the erosion of a unified national identity. By contrast, the ruling elites claim that Ethiopia's rapid economic growth will transcend ethnic divisions, as those benefiting from national progress will be less likely to identify primarily along ethnic lines. This study leveraged Afrobarometer survey data to examine these contrasting narratives. Our findings support the claims of the ruling elite, suggesting that Ethiopians with higher economic status tend to identify more strongly with their national identity than with their ethnic group. However, citizens' perceptions that their ethnic group is mistreated weaken the positive association between economic status and national identity. Furthermore, support for federalism, which likely arises from perceptions of mistreatment, strengthens ethnic identities. Based on these findings, we argue that fostering economic prosperity should be complemented by efforts to address perceived grievances, which are crucial for enhancing nation-building. To this end, policymakers should integrate narratives that promote institutional and generalized trust into educational curricula, thus fostering a sense of national unity and cohesion.

title: Collusive Communication in Bertrand Oligopolies: A Deep Learning Approach

detail.title: Collusive Communication in Bertrand Oligopolies: A Deep Learning Approach
detail.abstract: In this paper, I investigates the impact of explicit communication on collusive outcomes in Bertrand oligopoly markets by combining experimental economics with natural language processing (NLP) techniques. By using the experimental setup and chat deta of (Fonseca and Normann (2012)), I examine how varying the number of firms (n) influences pricesetting behaviors under Talk and NoTalk treatments. Employing Neural Topic Modeling (NTM) via the BERTopic framework and sentiment analysis of chat transcripts, I uncover linguistic drivers of collusion. Specifically, this study finds that mediumsized markets (n = 4) exhibit a notable capacity to sustain supracompetitive prices through highly focused trust-building, explicit coordination on collusive price targets, and consistently positive sentiment. In contrast, smaller duopolies risk fragile agreements due to high vulnerability to single-firm defections, while larger markets face coordination challenges stemming from dispersed accountability. By integrating experimental data with text-analytic methods, this study offers novel insights into the mechanisms by which explicit communication fosters collusion, which is vital for both theory and antitrust strategies. These results underscore the value of NLP-based approaches for detecting collusive "signatures," as they illuminate how and why participants use language to align on pricing, maintain trust, and discourage deviation within an oligopolistic context.

title: MDCEV Model-driven Causal Analysis on Teleworking During COVID-19: Evidence from Smartphone-based Panel Probe Person Data in Tokyo

detail.title: MDCEV Model-driven Causal Analysis on Teleworking During COVID-19: Evidence from Smartphone-based Panel Probe Person Data in Tokyo
detail.abstract: COVID-19 forced many workers to telework, altering their activity choices. In general, telework continued in many countries after the pandemic, so it is essential to consider its impact to predict the future behavior of residents. The investigation of the impact of telework on non-work activity choice behavior represents a critical research avenue; however, the existing literature in this area remains inconclusive. In this paper, we use longitudinal probe-person survey data from before and after the COVID-19 in Tokyo to determine the causal effect of teleworking on workers' nonworking activities. Focusing on trip frequency and activity time allocation, we conducted an analysis using the difference-in-differences method. The results showed that teleworking increased the number of activities near home on weekdays but did not significantly change the number of activities far from home. The time spent on each activity became shorter in all areas. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of activity time allocation using a mixed multiple discrete-continuous nested extreme value model reveals that teleworkers are more fixed in their activity location and less heterogeneous in their time consumption patterns than non-teleworkers. Teleworkers' weekday activities have changed to focus more on activities necessary for daily life than before the introduction of telework. This may have resulted in homogenizing activity locations and time consumption behaviors. From the results of this analysis, we will obtain implications regarding the importance of infrastructure and community facilities in areas with many teleworkers, and we will discuss the contribution of telework to data-driven urban development.

title: Fast and Slow Level Shifts in Intraday Stochastic Volatility

detail.title: Fast and Slow Level Shifts in Intraday Stochastic Volatility
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a mixed-frequency stochastic volatility model for intraday returns that captures fast and slow level shifts in the volatility level induced by news from both low-frequency variables and scheduled announcements. A MIDAS component describes slow-moving changes in volatility driven by daily variables, while an announcement component captures fast eventdriven volatility bursts. Using 5-minute crude oil futures returns, we show that accounting for both fast and slow level shifts significantly improves volatility forecasts at intraday and daily horizons. The superior forecasts also translate into higher Sharpe ratios using the volatilitymanaged portfolio strategy.

title: Regional and Neighboring Effects of Green Energy firms on Carbon Emissions: The Moderating Role of Environmental Policies and Innovation
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Milan, Polytechnic University of Milan - Dipartimento di Economia e Produzione, University of Bologna - Department of Management and Politecnico di Torino

detail.title: Regional and Neighboring Effects of Green Energy firms on Carbon Emissions: The Moderating Role of Environmental Policies and Innovation
detail.abstract: This study examines the role of green energy firms in reducing CO2 emissions by focusing on two dynamics: their direct effects within the firms’ own geographical areas and their indirect effects on neighbouring regions. Moreover, we assess whether environmental policies and the innovation activity of the area moderate the impact of green energy firms on CO2 emission reductions. Merging two unique datasets, respectively on European green energy firms, identified through a Machine Learning approach, and European environmental policies, we create a region-level panel dataset covering 235 European regions over the period 2000-2022, for a total of 5,405 observations. Using both a Fixed-Effect Model and a Spatial Durbin Model, we show that green energy firms reduce CO2 emissions within their home regions, with this effect being particularly pronounced in areas characterized by a stronger policy framework. Interestingly, results indicate that an increase in green energy firms in one region is associated with higher CO2 emissions in neighbouring regions. We also show that, in regions with limited innovation activity, green energy firms contribute more significantly to reducing CO2 emissions, whereas their marginal effect is lower in more innovation-intensive regions. Additionally, we find evidence of a nuanced policy effect. While we confirm the overall positive interaction between environmental policies and green energy firms in reducing emissions, we identify differences in effectiveness between market-based and non-market-based approaches, as well as evidence of carbon leakage effects in neighbouring regions.

title: Can global uncertainty factors explain the dynamics of climate-aligned ETFs?
affiliations: Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, , Notre Dame University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Department of Economics, Pusan National University

detail.title: Can global uncertainty factors explain the dynamics of climate-aligned ETFs?
detail.abstract: We study how global uncertainty transmits to climate‑aligned exchange‑traded funds (ETFs) across horizons and market states. Using monthly data for four ETFs—ICLN (clean energy), GUNR (natural resources), CGW (water), and ERTH (sustainable future)—and four uncertainty indices—VIX (equity), OVX (oil), GVZ (gold), and CPU (climate policy)—over September 2011–June 2025, we implement a hybrid framework that combines wavelet quantile correlation (WQC), quantile‑on‑quantile regression (QQR), and multivariate quantile regression (MQR). The main empirical results are as follows. (i) Transmission is scale‑dependent: short‑run returns respond mainly to financial and oil volatility (VIX, OVX), whereas long‑run spillovers are associated with structural risks (GVZ, CPU). (ii) Effects are nonlinear and asymmetric and concentrate in the return distribution’s tails; downside responses dominate, particularly for ICLN and ERTH in high‑volatility regimes. (iii) Sectoral heterogeneity matters: GUNR behaves procyclically and is sensitive to OVX; CGW is relatively defensive yet exposed to persistent CPU; ERTH shows joint sensitivity to financial and policy shocks. The granularity of these sectoral distinctions underscores the value of QQR over MQR: by preserving tail dependencies and joint‑quantile interactions that distributional averaging would smooth over, QQR enables more precise identification of vulnerability zones specific to each ETF's exposure profile. Policy implications can be summarized as:  (i) credible climate policy mitigates long-horizon risk; (ii) static diversification and mean-based risk models understate extreme losses in climate portfolios; and (iii) quantile-aware allocation is essential to manage regime-dependent exposures.

title: Monetary Policy Transmission to Household Credit

detail.title: Monetary Policy Transmission to Household Credit

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effectiveness of monetary policy transmission in developing countries using loan-level data from Uganda’s credit registry. We analyze more than 632,000 household loans issued by all commercial banks between 2017 and 2023, a period marked by significant policy rate fluctuations. We find that household credit, which accounts for over 50 percent of new loan accounts, responds to monetary policy: rate hikes are followed by higher lending rates and reduced loan size and maturity. Controlling for credit demand with time-varying borrower-group fixed effects, we find stronger transmission among banks with lower liquidity and capital, and those holding more government securities. The effects are more pronounced for fixed-rate loans than for floating-rate loans. In general, our results support the presence of a bank lending channel in Uganda, similar to what is observed in more advanced economies.

title: Not Fannie and Freddie: Wall Street's Trillion-Dollar Fraud Machine Inside the Machines of Mortgage Madness, Derivatives, and the CDS Time Bomb
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Not Fannie and Freddie: Wall Street's Trillion-Dollar Fraud Machine Inside the Machines of Mortgage Madness, Derivatives, and the CDS Time Bomb
detail.abstract: This paper challenges the conventional narrative that government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) and affordable housing policies caused the 2008 financial crisis. Through detailed analysis of the origination, securitization, and distribution chain, I demonstrate that private-label mortgage-backed securities and the unregulated credit default swap market were the primary drivers of the crisis. The evidence shows that toxic loan products-including no-documentation loans and hybrid adjustable-rate mortgages with payment shocks exceeding 70%-were deliberately engineered by private originators operating under perverse fee-based incentive structures. Investment banks securitized these loans while conducting inadequate due diligence, creating complex collateralized debt obligations that amplified systemic risk. The $62 trillion credit default swap market, particularly AIG's $500 billion in mortgagerelated exposure, transformed a housing bubble into a global financial catastrophe through counterparty contagion. GSE participation in risky lending came late (2005-2007) and remained modest compared to private-sector dominance. Analysis of the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse failures reveals that fundamental vulnerabilities-liquidity mismatches, concentration risk, regulatory forbearance, and moral hazard-persist fifteen years later, suggesting regulatory reforms have addressed symptoms while leaving causal mechanisms largely intact.

detail.abstract: ESG activities are a forward-looking measure to prevent risks from negative externalities. Linking ESG scores with the crude oil market, we assess their mitigating effect on returns during periods of rising oil price volatility. We examine the interplay between ESG scores and crude oil volatility’s impact on returns. Interestingly, this interaction transforms ESG into an insurance-like hedge, protecting returns as volatility increases. Notably, we identify a pivotal turning point at relatively low volatility levels. Below this threshold, ESG activities lack effectiveness, but when volatility surpasses it, their hedging power becomes pronounced. This effect intensifies as volatility rises, rewarding ESG leaders more significantly. Our sectoral and quantile analyses corroborate these findings. Overall, our findings support the role of ESG activities as a “safe haven” in times of financial turmoil, focusing its contribution to the interplay between ESG and oil volatility on periods of heightened uncertainty in the crude oil market.

detail.title: The Tenth Anniversary of Marriage Equality: How Traditional Marriage Law Led to Constitutional Protection for Same-Sex Marriage

publicationDetails.detailsText: 3 Journal of American Constitutional History 899 (2025). https://doi.org/10.59015/jach.URIP8173
SMU Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 711
publicationDetails.journalName: Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This essay explores how the history of interstate marriage recognition law was central to the Supreme Court’s recognition of constitutional protection for the right of same-sex couples to marry. Prior to the 1990s, there were essentially no laws on same-sex marriage in the United States. That changed in the 1990s, when the Hawaii Supreme Court issued a ruling in Baehr v. Lewin that made authorization of same-sex marriage seem inevitable in that state. The threat fueled the adoption first of the federal Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) in 1996 and then mini-DOMAs in most states. Those laws were broad and unprecedented. DOMA singled out one type of marriage for nonrecognition under any federal law or program, while most federal laws do not provide definitions of marriage, even where marital status is highly relevant such as in eligibility for spousal Social Security benefits. Rather, Congress has traditionally deferred to state law determinations of personal status when applying federal laws. State DOMAs prohibited the celebration of same-sex marriages within their borders and recognition of those celebrated elsewhere. These laws were also unprecedented in that they barred interstate recognition of all same-sex marriages without any consideration of the common-law rules that usually drove such determinations. The departures from the usual approach to federal-state and interstate marriage recognition provided a doctrinal hook for constitutional protection. Although the Supreme Court recognized the right of same-sex couples to marry in Obergefell v. Hodges in 2015, the key inroad was its decision in Windsor v. United States, two years earlier. In Windsor, the Court struck down the federal law provision of DOMA based on the idea that discrimination of an unusual character raises the specter of animus—and animus cannot be the sole justification for a valid governmental action, even when the targeted group has not been recognized as a suspect or quasi-suspect class. The same argument was then used to attack the state DOMAs. The “discrimination of an unusual character” was the legislatures’ blunt and categorical non-recognition of same-sex marriages, despite strong histories in most states of granting recognition to marriages that were validly celebrated elsewhere despite strong opposition within the state. The opponents of same-sex marriage unwittingly undermined their own cause by enacting such unprecedented and unforgiving nonrecognition laws.

title: The Effect of a Woman-Friendly Occupation on Employment: U.S. Postmasters Before World War II

detail.title: The Effect of a Woman-Friendly Occupation on Employment: U.S. Postmasters Before World War II

keywords: Women's Employment in the Historical United States

detail.abstract: This paper studies the postmaster occupation in the early 20th-century United States, a rare opportunity for women to earn relatively high pay with flexible hours at a time when comparable positions were scarce. Using a novel dataset linking postmaster appointments to census records, I show that these woman-friendly positions attracted educated and qualified White women into the labor market. However, RD results indicate that many women exited the labor force after their appointments ended, with only a few transitioning into other skilled occupations, accounting for just one-third of the 24 pp. employment loss. The scarcity of jobs comparable to postmasters, combined with broader labor market constraints such as marriage bars and the Great Depression, likely limited the long-term gains of this otherwise advantageous occupation.

title: Bloc Control and Contestability in Decentralized Governance: Evidence from the Arbitrum Network
affiliations: King’s College London - King's Business School

detail.title: Bloc Control and Contestability in Decentralized Governance: Evidence from the Arbitrum Network
detail.abstract: Decentralized autonomous organisations (DAOs) are increasingly utilized to manage on-chain resources and communities of blockchain ecosystems. To address participation issues, several protocols have introduced intermediated decision-making in the form of delegation schemes. Inspired by the concept of liquid democracy, they represent tools that blend direct and representative decision-making. While delegation yields results in encouraging broader token holder participation, it introduces the risk of misalignment and entrenchment, resembling agency conflicts in traditional corporate governance. Both ownership and control of DAOs have been shown to centralize around influential addresses. This paper draws on a common substrate in the literature on the alignment of both algorithmic and corporate decision-making processes-contestability-to derive the main research question: "Does governance contestability promote accountable and engaged decision-making in DAOs?" This paper proposes contestability as the optimal mode of coordinating decision-making in decentralized governance systems. In contributing to the literature on decentralized governance, it is expected that this paper defines the main mechanism of token holder engagement and delegate alignment in decentralized governance.

title: Spiral Phase-Space Representation of Financial Instability: A Complex Number Visualization Framework

detail.title: Spiral Phase-Space Representation of Financial Instability: A Complex Number Visualization Framework
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel visual and mathematical framework for representing macroeconomic instability through complex-number phase-space dynamics. By mapping real economic output and financial credit into a two-dimensional complex plane, economic cycles emerge as logarithmic spirals rather than linear or cyclical trends. This approach bridges Hyman Minsky's Financial Instability Hypothesis with the geometric formalism of complex analysis, offering both predictive and explanatory power for economic crises. The model provides an intuitive visualization of leverage accumulation and instability growth, transforming macroeconomic data into a dynamic spiral system.
