detail.abstract: This qualitative study examines how globalization impacts the emergence and development of women entrepreneurs in Central Asia. The study also focuses on global tools, platforms, and opportunities to support women in launching and growing their own businesses, as well as what kinds of challenges they continue to face. The findings of this study showed that globalization has opened up significant pathways for entrepreneurial growth, especially through digital technologies and international networks. However, many women continue to encounter structural inequalities, lack of mentorship, and societal expectations that hinder their full participation in the business world. This study also recommends offering more practical training, encouraging partnerships between women in different countries, and using online communities to help women connect, learn, and grow their businesses.

title: Can A Wealth Tax Reduce CO2 Emissions in Europe?
affiliations: University of Greenwich and University of Greenwich

detail.title: Can A Wealth Tax Reduce CO2 Emissions in Europe?
detail.abstract: We analyse the potential of wealth taxes to reduce CO2 emissions through two transmission channels: the inequality channel, which links reductions in wealth inequality to lower emissions, and the consumption channel, which analyses how wealth taxes affect consumption by top wealth holders. We simulate the effects of various wealth tax designs over one- and ten-year horizons using harmonised microdata from 22 European countries. Our analysis accounts for survey non-response bias, heterogeneous rates of returns across households, and behavioural responses to taxation. We find that, through the inequality channel, an annual progressive wealth tax could reduce annual CO2 emissions by 7.5%–14.7% after ten years relative to a no-tax scenario, depending on tax progressivity. Through the consumption channel, the average reduction is between 1.5%–3.6%. These findings highlight the potential of wealth taxes to serve a dual purpose: curbing wealth concentration and contributing meaningfully to climate mitigation and justice, by focusing on high-net worth households who account for a disproportionate share of emissions.

title: Regression and Forecasting of U.S. Stock Returns Based on Multiple Linear Regression Model and LSTM-GA: Take the Manuf, Hitec, and Other Sectors as Examples

detail.title: Regression and Forecasting of U.S. Stock Returns Based on Multiple Linear Regression Model and LSTM-GA: Take the Manuf, Hitec, and Other Sectors as Examples
detail.abstract: In today's era dominated by vast data, novel methodologies are increasingly employed for forecasting stock returns. This paper focuses on the investment returns of three specific sectors within the U.S. stock market: Manufacturing, High Technology, and Other. We evaluate the effectiveness of three different models: the Fama-French threefactor model, the Carhart four-factor model, and the Fama-French five-factor model, across these sectors. Additionally, the study explores the application of an LSTM model to uncover additional factors that may impact stock returns.The empirical results reveal that the Fama-French five-factor model demonstrates superior validity in predicting the returns of the three sectors analyzed. Moreover, the LSTM model showcases its capability to capture specific factors influencing returns in certain industries, thereby enhancing its utility for regression and prediction of stock returns in these areas. This study provides insightful benchmarks and could serve as a robust model for future projections of stock returns, demonstrating the potential of combining traditional factor models with advanced machine learning techniques.

title: "Giving Up": The Impact of Decreasing Housing Affordability on Consumption, Work Effort, and Investment
affiliations: Northwestern University and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: "Giving Up": The Impact of Decreasing Housing Affordability on Consumption, Work Effort, and Investment
detail.abstract: Housing affordability has declined sharply in recent decades, leading many younger generations to give up on homeownership. Using a calibrated life-cycle model matched to U.S. data, we project that the cohort born in the 1990s will reach retirement with a homeownership rate roughly 9.6 percentage points lower than that of their parents' generation. The model also shows that as households' perceived probability of attaining homeownership falls, they systematically shift their behavior: they consume more relative to their wealth, reduce work effort, and take on riskier investments. We show empirically that renters with relatively low wealth exhibit the same patterns. These responses compound over the life cycle, producing substantially greater wealth dispersion between those who retain hope of homeownership and those who give up. We propose a targeted subsidy that lifts the largest number of young renters above the "giving-up threshold." This policy yields welfare gains that are 3.2 times those of a uniform transfer and 10.3 times those of a transfer targeted to the bottom 10% of the wealth distribution, while also increasing homeownership rate, raising work effort, and reducing reliance on the social safety net.

title: Five Shades of Grey: Antitrust & Labor Market World Tour
affiliations: Universidade de Brasília (UnB) and Pinheiro Neto Advogados

detail.title: Five Shades of Grey: Antitrust & Labor Market World Tour
detail.abstract: This article explores the evolving intersection between antitrust law and labor market regulation and investigations across a range of global jurisdictions. Once considered a marginal area of enforcement, labor market practices—such as (1) wage fixing, (2) no-poach agreements, (3) information exchanges, (4) non-compete clauses and (5) non-solicitation agreements—are now attracting growing scrutiny from competition authorities worldwide. Drawing on developments from the Australia, Belgium, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, European Union, France, Greece, Hungary, Lithuania, Mexico, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, United Kingdom, United States, the article maps the diverse legal frameworks and enforcement trends addressing employer coordination and restrictions on worker mobility. Through a comparative lens, the study analyzes how traditional boundaries between labor and competition law are dissolving, prompting new regulatory paradigms and enforcement strategies. It highlights the implications of this convergence for worker welfare, economic freedom, and the future of antitrust law in a labor-constrained global economy.

title: Private Credit: What Do We Know?
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: Private Credit: What Do We Know?
detail.abstract: The explosive growth of private credit over the past fifteen years has attracted the attention of an increasing number of policymakers and academic researchers. This paper provides an overview of the large-sample research to date, structured around three core themes: the distinct economic function of private credit, the macroeconomic implications of the expansion of private debt, and the evaluation of private debt as an asset class. It highlights areas where there is convincing evidence, such as the overall exposure of the banking sector to private credit, and outlines several other areas, such as the interplay between monetary policy and private credit or the evolution of underwriting standards, where the evidence remains limited. Finally, the paper situates the evolution of high-yield debt markets, including private credit, within a historical context, highlighting their fundamental connection to the evolution of private equity industry.

title: Forecasting Long Run Earnings Growth for Global Asset Allocation
affiliations: University of Bristol, , University of Bristol Business School and University of Bristol Business School

detail.title: Forecasting Long Run Earnings Growth for Global Asset Allocation

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by Innovate UK [project number 10077271].

detail.abstract: We develop a parsimonious model of aggregate earnings growth that incorporates information contained in market prices, accounting data and analysts' consensus forecasts. Using a panel regression framework, we implement the model to forecast long run earnings growth for a sample of 42 MSCI markets and six MSCI regions over the period 1998 to 2025. The model explains 32 percent of the out-of-sample variation in earnings growth at the market level and 43 percent at the region level. Each of the three sources-market prices, accounting data and analysts' forecasts-contain significant incremental information about future earnings growth, and the model outperforms commonly used naïve forecasts of earnings growth in terms of accuracy, bias, efficiency and information content. The model offers a practical framework for forecasting aggregate long run earnings growth for the purpose of global asset allocation.

title: Entrepreneurship Policy and the Wealth of Nations
affiliations: University of Louisville

detail.title: Entrepreneurship Policy and the Wealth of Nations

declarations.funderStatement: Beloit College Upton Miller Forum

detail.abstract: In this paper, I examine these two approaches to entrepreneurship policy, outlining their theoretical foundations and providing a concise summary of the empirical evidence supporting each. As part of this assessment, I draw on Baumol’s (1990) framework of productive and unproductive entrepreneurship as a lens to evaluate how different policy approaches influence the allocation of entrepreneurial effort and the implication for socioeconomic development. Empirical evidence suggests that the laissez-faire approach to entrepreneurship policy, characterized by higher levels of economic freedom, is a significant driver of productive entrepreneurial activity and innovation across countries and regions (Bennett and Nikolaev 2019). In contrast, the evidence on the efficacy of interventionist entrepreneurial finance schemes is more nuanced (Dvouletý et al. 2021). While such policies have been associated with productive outcomes, including increased innovation and follow-on private investment in specific contexts, they have also been linked to unproductive outcomes, such as crowding out private investment and fostering subsidy-dependent entrepreneurship in others (Lerner 2009). These findings suggest that effective entrepreneurship policy requires a careful balance between fostering economic freedom and selectively addressing market gaps to maximize productive entrepreneurship while minimizing distortions that encourage unproductive entrepreneurship.

title: Financial Systems in the Digital Era: Technological Shifts in Liquidity, Payments, and Stability
affiliations: Regional Advisory Commision on Financial Markets

detail.title: Financial Systems in the Digital Era: Technological Shifts in Liquidity, Payments, and Stability
detail.abstract:
Digital technologies redefine liquidity, payment systems, and stability. Central banks and financial authorities monitor risks. Overall risk does not diminish—only channels shift.

Research questions arise. How does technology change market structure? Which institutional gaps demand attention?

Liquid financial ecosystems underpin economic stability. Ancillary instruments—regulatory capital, management guidance—help constrain outright risk-taking. The 2007–09 global financial crisis demonstrated that liquidity facilities alone do not assure robust liquidity management by firms [1]. New channels for central bank liquidity and the modalities underpinning liquidity provisioning merit examination. How does liquidity hoarding transmit stress to the broader economy? Can advances to firms under stress spark contagion across sectors instead? Which actions enhance liquidity resilience?

Digital markets transform liquidity provisioning. Streaming liquidity services and programmable liquidity instruments enable agents to dynamically fund investments across markets according to changing conditions and preferences. Streaming liquidity allows market participants with access to rapidly updated transaction data to establish funding or financing arrangements conditional on real-time variables such as price, volatility, open interest, or on-chain activity. Agents procuring funding with these tools are not locked into a fixed obligation. They can increase, decrease, or offset positions based on evolving circumstances. Programmable liquidity enables similar flexibility within tightly defined parameters but without streaming requirements. New provisioning modalities reshape the efficacy and desirability of funding.

Rapid quote submission, hidden-limit orders, and a high share of algorithmic trading signal conditions across underlying asset classes. The quote flashes or removal, along with the adoption or withdrawal of circulating funding or financing, transmit information about evolving demand for liquidity [2]. Automated strategies can shift rapidly among collateralised venues; the choice of collateral depends on conditions in the funding, financing, and derivatives markets. These relationships also transmit information; high-frequency trading across multiple underlying markets can instantaneously reveal interdependencies across diverse asset classes and jurisdictions. Fast, dynamic automated strategies amplify the policy apparatus and adjust liquidity positioning in response to macro or geopolitical disruptions influenced by central bank, fiscal, or monetary policies [3].

title: Are Bidder-Initiated Takeovers Opportunistic?
affiliations: Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, University of Southern California and Norwegian School of Economics

detail.title: Are Bidder-Initiated Takeovers Opportunistic?
detail.abstract: By initiating the takeover process and paying for the target with temporarily overpriced shares, acquirers may successfully outbid even more efficient buyers. We present some first tests of this opportunistic market-timing hypothesis that requires the bidder - not the target - to initiate the deal process. The endogenous initiation-decision is treated as rational side-bets in otherwise synergistic takeovers. The empirical challenge, which we address, is to separate such opportunistic side-bets from rational payment design, where stock-financing hedges against target adverse selection. Evidence from reduced-form regressions, structural estimation, and wealth effects suggests that bidder-initiated and stock-financed takeovers primarily hedge against target adverse selection.

title: Plastic Island: A Wake-Up Call from the Deep

detail.title: Plastic Island: A Wake-Up Call from the Deep
detail.abstract: Plastic Island: A Wake-Up Call from the Deep is a powerful 2021 documentary directed by Duerre Panne that exposes the devastating impact of plastic pollution on our planet. The film combines scientific research, expert interviews, and personal stories from affected communities to create a compelling narrative about humanity’s dependence on plastic and its far-reaching consequences. Told through a thematic structure, the documentary explores the origins, spread, and effects of plastic waste, while also highlighting efforts to seek sustainable solutions. Its strong visuals, emotional pacing, and well-crafted sound design deepen the viewer’s connection to the issue. Ultimately, Plastic Island is not just an informative film—it’s a call to action. It urges audiences to reflect on their everyday habits and recognize that the fight against plastic pollution begins with individual responsibility and collective change.

title: Valuation Models
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, Arizona State University (ASU) - Finance Department and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Valuation Models
detail.abstract: Valuation models lie at the core of both financial theory and practice, yet we lack systematic evidence on how professionals value assets, which models perform best, and why. To make progress on these questions, we analyze valuation models in 1.1 million equity analyst reports. While, on average, simpler multiples-based models generate more accurate forecasts than more complex discounted cash flow (DCF) models, this masks important heterogeneity: skilled analysts produce superior forecasts with DCF models, especially for hard-to-value firms, underscoring the importance of expertise when employing complex models. To establish that model-specific expertise matters, we exploit a quasi-exogenous shock that forced some analysts to switch valuation models, and show that their forecast accuracy subsequently declines relative to analysts with established experience using the new approach. This highlights a fundamental trade-off between simplicity and sophistication in valuation, where optimal method choice depends on analyst characteristics, such as skill. Finally, given their unconditional superior performance, we study how analysts determine multiples. Analysts use historical, current, and peer-based reference points to contextualize their choice of multiples, but they do not use these benchmarks mechanically when determining their prices. Moreover, we show that sensitivity analyses have become increasingly common, bull and bear scenarios are asymmetric and account for greater downside risk, and their inclusion is associated with more conservative forecasts.

title: International Investing: Diversification and Beyond

detail.abstract: We develop a framework for analyzing individual stocks across two countries to uncover international investment gains arising from (i) differences in global factor risk premia and (ii) country-specific factors unavailable domestically. Applying the method to individual stocks in 27 countries from 1966 to 2022, we find large and robust opportunities. Investing in country-specific factor portfolios more than triple the Sharpe ratio of a US market-index investor, and strategies that exploit crosscountry differences in common factor premia are similarly profitable-even among G7 markets-challenging the view of completely integrated global equity markets.

title: Exchange Rate Volatility and Balance-Sheet FX Exposure in Emerging Economies
affiliations: World Bank Group Ecosystem

detail.title: Exchange Rate Volatility and Balance-Sheet FX Exposure in Emerging Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed in the Treasury Department of the World Bank Group. However, this research was conducted independently as an academic contribution and does not represent the views or policies of the World Bank Group or any of its affiliates.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how exchange rate volatility affects corporate and sovereign balance sheets in emerging markets (EMs) with significant foreign-currency exposure. Using a conceptual balance-sheet framework, it quantifies how currency depreciation translates into valuation losses depending on asset-liability mismatches. The analysis finds that a 10% depreciation can erode corporate net worth by 3-4%, with highly leveraged or importdependent economies facing the steepest declines. The results underscore the dual nature of exchange rate flexibility-it absorbs shocks but also magnifies financial vulnerabilities when balance sheets are unhedged. Policy implications focus on strengthening macroprudential tools, promoting natural hedging, and improving market depth.

title: Chapter One: Two Countries, Three Industries, Ten Stories. Global Business and Local Struggle
affiliations: , University of Melbourne, University of Melbourne School of Social and Political Sciences, RMIT University and University of Newcastle (Australia) - Newcastle Law School

detail.title: Chapter One: Two Countries, Three Industries, Ten Stories. Global Business and Local Struggle

declarations.ethicsApproval: Melbourne Univesity 1137194

detail.abstract:
This introductory chapter of the book, Global Business and Local Struggle: Reimagining Non Judicial Remedy for Human Rights, summarises ten case studies detailing the use of Non-Judicial Mechanisms (NJMs) by communities in India and Indonesia to seek redress for human rights violations in the mining, agriculture, and apparel sectors.

The overarching finding is that NJMs are no panacea and significant human rights violations often persisted. However, partial success was observed when NJMs were used as part of a wider, multifaceted array of strategies. Communities employed NJMs to achieve modest goals, such as generating public scrutiny, embarrassing state regulators, or gaining leverage against companies.

The effectiveness of redress was deeply shaped by local context:

  • Local Business Elites exerted strong political influence, often minimizing NJM accountability.

  • State Institutions presented obstacles due to India's lengthy judicial processes and Indonesia's corruption and weak enforcement.

  • Success depended on strong local support and connection to established civil society groups.

Case studies involving the CAO, NCPs, and the ETI confirm that NJM intervention, while rarely achieving full remedy, sometimes led to positive outcomes like compensation, increased public scrutiny, or policy changes, but these were often narrow and isolated. The persistence of systemic violations highlights the limits of current transnational accountability efforts.

title: Global Interest Rate Shocks and Emerging Market Sovereign Spreads: Evidence from Panel Analysis

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how global interest rate shocks-particularly U.S. monetary tightening-affect sovereign spreads in emerging markets (EMs). Using a conceptual panel regression framework, the analysis quantifies spillovers from changes in U.S. 10-year Treasury yields to EM sovereign spreads. The results suggest that a 100-basis-point increase in global yields widens EM spreads by 45-70 basis points over two quarters, with higher sensitivity in economies that have elevated external debt and weaker reserve buffers. The findings highlight how global financial conditions shape EM financing costs and underscore the importance of fiscal credibility and debt management for mitigating spillover effects.

title: Strategic Patenting Under Financial Disclosure Mandates
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Strategic Patenting Under Financial Disclosure Mandates
detail.abstract: We examine how financial disclosure regulations influence firms' intellectual property (IP) protection strategies. While disclosure enhances transparency, it also exposes firms to competitive risks by revealing insights into their product market performance. We develop a model of strategic patenting that jointly embeds financial and patent disclosure. Our model predicts that increased financial transparency raises the risk of not patenting, compelling firms to lower their patenting threshold. This effect, which leads to more patent filings of lower average quality, is predicted to dominate as long as financial and patent disclosures are substitutes or not strongly complementary. We test these predictions using the ASC 606's revenue disaggregation requirements. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that affected firms file significantly more patents after the announcement, and the average quality of new patents declines. We also find that the effects are stronger for firms that historically rely more on patenting for protection and for firms with more opaque ex-ante information environments.

title: Term Structure of Interest Rates and Monetary Policy Transmission in Developed and Emerging Markets
affiliations: World Bank Group Ecosystem

detail.title: Term Structure of Interest Rates and Monetary Policy Transmission in Developed and Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: This paper examines the transmission of monetary policy through the term structure of interest rates across developed and emerging markets. Using a conceptual framework based on the Nelson-Siegel-Svensson (NSS) yield-curve model, the study quantifies how policy rate changes affect yields across maturities. Results indicate that policy transmission is rapid and nearly complete in advanced economies but partial and delayed in emerging markets. The paper attributes these differences to market segmentation, liquidity constraints, and expectations formation. The findings offer valuable insights for policymakers seeking to strengthen monetary transmission mechanisms and for Treasury and ALM practitioners managing duration and interest-rate exposure.

title: Is Monetary Policy Still Seasonal?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Is Monetary Policy Still Seasonal?

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
A 2012 Liberty Street Economics post noted that U.S. monetary policy exhibits a surprising degree of seasonal behavior: over the 1987-2008 period, the Federal Reserve was much more likely to lower interest rates (or abstain from raising rates) in the first month of each quarter than in the two subsequent months. Thirteen years later, we revisit that analysis to investigate whether the seasonal pattern in monetary policy still holds today, in the wake of a rate hiking cycle, a pandemic, a surge in inflation, and a second round of rate hikes. We find that the pattern has indeed continued; however, unlike in the earlier sample period, it can be completely explained by the timing of the FOMC calendar.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2025/11/is-monetary-policy-still-seasonal/

title: The Role of LGUs and Recycling Provisions in Solid Waste Management
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Role of LGUs and Recycling Provisions in Solid Waste Management
detail.abstract:
Solid waste management has long been one of the most pressing environmental challenges in the Philippines, primarily due to rapid urbanization, population growth, and the increasing volume of household and industrial waste. To address this issue, the government enacted Republic Act No. 9003, also known as the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000. This legislation establishes a comprehensive framework for waste reduction, segregation, recycling, and disposal (Republic Act No. 9003, 2000).
This critique focuses on Section 10 (Role of Local Government Units), Article 4 (Recycling), Sections 30, 36, 37, and 39, and Chapter VI (Penal Provisions). It argues that while RA 9003 provides a solid foundation for sustainable waste management, it faces major challenges in enforcement and implementation due to inadequate resources, limited technical capacity, and weak local compliance.

title: The Role of Financial Data as a Macro-Financial Asset: Evidence from India’s UPI, Aadhaar Ecosystem, and Digital Lending Sector

detail.title: The Role of Financial Data as a Macro-Financial Asset: Evidence from India’s UPI, Aadhaar Ecosystem, and Digital Lending Sector
detail.abstract: India's digital public infrastructure-built on UPI, Aadhaar, and the Account Aggregator ecosystem-has turned financial data into a powerful, economy-shaping resource. This paper asks: does India's experience prove that financial data is a public good, benefiting all, or a private asset, reinforcing control by powerful actors? Drawing on Laura Veldkamp's influential framework, as well as global macro-finance research, the analysis demonstrates that India's approach to digital infrastructure uniquely blends public and market logic. Case studies of UPI adoption, Aadhaarbased microfinance, and digital lending regulations reveal both tremendous gains in inclusion and new systemic risks. Evidence shows that while digital rails lower barriers to formal credit and economic security, they can also concentrate power and amplify inequalities if left unchecked. By comparing India with other emerging markets, the study argues that India offers a live experiment in how societies can choose to shape financial data as either a collective asset for macro stability or as a rent-generating tool for private actors. The conclusion offers policy prescriptions so that future growth is inclusive, resilient, and grounded in data equity-ensuring that the assetization of financial data serves the many.

title: Selling Supplemental Information

detail.title: Selling Supplemental Information
detail.abstract: I consider an environment in which a decision maker faces uncertainty and privately holds information in the form of a signal about the true state of the world. The decision maker purchases additional information from a data broker before receiving the signal realization.  I characterize the data broker’s optimal selling mechanism, which involves screening over all possible signals. I allow the space of all signals the data broker can sell to be arbitrarily correlated with the signal the decision maker owns. This plays a key role in designing the optimal menu. In the binary-action setting, the data broker extracts the efficient surplus by offering a distinct binary signal for each type. Moreover, this result holds even when the broker does not know the prior distribution over states. In more general environments, I provide conditions on the payoff structure and the decision maker’s type space under which the data broker extracts the efficient surplus. I discuss scenarios in which efficient-surplus extraction is not possible.

detail.abstract:
This penultimate chapter of Global Business and Local Struggle: Reimagining Non-Judicial Remedy for Human Rights assesses the impact of Non-Judicial Mechanisms (NJMs) on human rights struggles in the context of transnational business activities, drawing on extensive empirical analysis. The core finding confirms the widespread failure of NJMs to achieve direct, rights-compliant redress, suggesting that narrowly evaluating them against human rights norms yields a "resounding answer: almost never."

However, adopting a "fields-of-struggle" lens reveals that NJMs can function as peripheral, strategic interventions that contribute to progressive change. Their utility lies not in substituting for judicial or state action, but in interacting with broader regulatory processes to produce cascading, indirect benefits (e.g., enhanced normative legitimacy, alliance building, media amplification).

The effectiveness of NJM intervention is therefore highly contingent, depending less on narrow procedural compliance (UN OHCHR 2011) and more on the extent to which aggrieved communities and their allies can strategically utilize NJMs to harness countervailing sources of financial, political, and discursive power (Drahos & Braithwaite 2000; Ruggie 2017). This analysis highlights that "success" is most likely when NJMs tip the balance within contested power struggles, emphasizing that effective redress requires a web of pressure incorporating judicial and non-judicial avenues.

detail.abstract: This article offers the first systematic evaluation of the Human Rights (Jersey) Law 2000 (HRJL), twenty-five years after its enactment. Using court judgments, States Assembly debates, scrutiny reports and government documents, it applies Joshua Newman’s four evaluative dimensions—objectives, tools, distributional outcomes and political impact—to a constitutional statute. The record is mixed. Rights feature in litigation and legislative process but enforcement is patchy and access limited by restrictive legal aid. Institutions are sparse: there is no commissioner, no committee, and only a short-lived programme of public legal education. Distribution is uneven: foreign offenders and financial actors have mobilised rights most effectively, while women and low-income groups are largely absent. Politically, incorporation has proved stable but low-salience, with rights almost invisible in elections, Assembly debate, and civil society. The study concludes that the HRJL has delivered stability without salience, entrenchment without civic depth.

detail.abstract: In order to maximize productivity, accountability, and overall success, performance management is a thorough and ongoing organizational process that aims to connect individual, team, and organizational goals. By guaranteeing that workers are given the freedom to participate successfully and possibilities for professional development, it acts as a pillar for creating a high-performance culture. Goal setting, where precise, quantifiable, and attainable objectives are created in accordance with the organization's strategic vision, is one of the interconnected elements that form the basis of this process. In order to measure progress and identify obstacles, managers and staff conduct regular reviews through continuous performance monitoring. A key component of the process is coaching and feedback, which provide staff members with helpful insights into their areas of strength and growth while facilitating two-way communication to promote cooperation and trust. The emphasis on staff development, which is accomplished through focused training programs, mentorship opportunities, and skill enhancement efforts, is an essential component of performance management. Periodically conducted formal performance evaluations offer organized insights into employee contributions, assisting in the identification of high performers, the filling of skill gaps, and the creation of specialized improvement plans for underperformers. Additionally, systems for rewards and recognition are combined to recognize exceptional work, increase drive, and promote consistent achievement. Through tools like balanced scorecards, 360-degree feedback mechanisms, and performance assessment systems, which assist organizations in measuring and analyzing performance metrics comprehensively, performance management also integrates data-driven decision-making. Leaders can use these systems to spot patterns, foresee problems, and put plans in place for ongoing development. In the end, performance management goes beyond the conventional idea of recurring performance evaluations. It is a constant and dynamic process intended to promote engagement, match employee contributions with organizational goals, and establish an atmosphere at work that supports continual learning and growth. Performance management improves organizational effectiveness by emphasizing accountability, transparency, and adaptability. This promotes long-term success in the cutthroat and quickly changing corporate environment of today.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of enhanced internet infrastructure on intra-city income inequality in China under the Broadband China Strategic Program (2014-2016). Employing a staggered difference-indifference methodology, we find that the program substantially reduced intra-city income inequality of the demonstration cities, measured by a notable 0.037point reduction in their Gini coefficients. This effect was primarily driven by income gains among low-and middle-income households, particularly in labor income. Our mechanism analysis further reveals that improved internet infrastructure facilitated new employment opportunities in the service sector and empowered low-skilled workers to transition to higher-paying roles within the platform economy. Our findings underscore the internet's potential to reduce inequality and promote inclusive labor markets, offering valuable policy insights for infrastructure investment and social equity in developing countries.

detail.abstract: This paper presents an evaluation framework that compares monetary exchange with non‑monetary compensation (time credits, reputation points, ledger‑based clearing) under an explicit notion of compensation recognition. The framework aggregates five dimensions—deadline reliability, participation scale and heterogeneity, new‑value creation, preservation of meaning and narrative, and settlement finality—and applies them to cases to estimate welfare differences. Results indicate that money dominates when urgency and scale are high, whereas non‑monetary compensation dominates when small‑scale contexts and reputation are strong. The boundary is design‑movable. We provide an operational procedure for including meaning and narrative in assessment from the perspective of information‑culture studies.

detail.abstract: This article traces the evolving state of major international regulatory responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically the 2024 IHR and the 2025 WHO Pandemic Agreement. It identifies a shift in the emphasis on the role of intellectual property on access to medicines and pandemic-related products to a myriad of other factors. The two instruments embody novel approaches to reposition the global public health for pandemic prevention, preparedness and response. Premised on good health and well-being, the instruments strengthen the SDGs, especially SDG 3, within the mainstream of global public health. With new and extended powers, the WHO is at the centre of this current transition in global health. However, there is no commensurate buffer for the organization to navigate the unassailable political obstacles to its new roles. Attempts to entrench equity and solidarity as the hallmark of the new global health order are unlikely to be far-reaching, being framed in politically constraining diplomatese. Specifically, the WHO Member States have yet to demonstrate temperance on the issue of sovereignty. Yet, the 2024 IHR and the 2025 WHO-PA encapsulate a strategic and principles-driven response to global health in a state of flux and in need of continually responsive nimbleness.

detail.abstract: The main purpose of this study was to assess teachers’ inclusive education practices and challenges in secondary schools of Gambella Region. To achieve the intended purpose, descriptive survey design was used which was supplemented by qualitative research to enrich data. The study was carried out in six purposively selected secondary schools of Gambella region and hence, teachers, school leaders and students with physical disabilities were selected as respondents by purposive and census sampling techniques respectively. Questionnaire was the main instrument of data collection. Observation, focus group discussion and document analysis were also utilized to substantiate the data obtained through the questionnaire. The data obtained through questionnaire was analyzed quantitatively using statistical tools such as percentage, mean, standard deviation, average means and T-test while data obtained by focus group discussion, observation, open-ended questions and document analysis were analyzed qualitatively.  As a result, findings suggested that secondary school teachers have diverse conceptualizations of inclusive education. Whereas, teachers’ attitude towards students with visual, hearing, speech impairment and mobility disability was found the most negative.  Findings also revealed that Gambella secondary school teachers’ practice of individualized education plan, adjustment of instructional strategies to meet the individual needs of learners was found to be inefficient and not responsive to the needs of students with physical disabilities. Furthermore, regarding teaching strategies, teachers used a variety of teaching methods in the inclusive classes both traditional and modern strategies. While implementing inclusive education, teachers encountered enormous challenges in practicing inclusive education due to their inadequate knowledge and limited professional development scopes. The challenges for teachers with in inclusive education practice are likely the result of insufficient knowledge, lack of training and attitude in relation to students with disabilities and professional support. Finally based on the findings and conclusions of the study recommendations forwarded that capacity building, strengthening awareness raising activities, promoting inclusive education curriculum, provision of appropriate teaching learning materials should be made for teachers by Gambella Education Bureau with near colleges and university who work on the area of inclusive education. To welcome students with disabilities into the regular class, classroom teachers need to give due attention to the development of individualized education programme. Further research on the area of curriculum differentiation and individualized Education programme was also recommended.

detail.abstract: This systematic review investigates the potential of executive dashboards and data visualization to reshape decision-making in the educational system of Ghana. Despite enhancements such as the Education Management Information System (EMIS), executives are faced with issues such as enrollment, asset allocation, and performance tracking since the data is fragmented. We reviewed 18 studies from 2015 to 2025 that we located after searching the Scopus and Web of Science databases using PRISMA. We located seminal knowledge about intuitive designs, governing with capability, robust IT systems, adoption issues, and virtues such as greater transparency and efficiency. We recommend an adapted architecture for the nation with a National KPI Catalogue, seamless integrated data with no holes, equity-oriented charts, predictive analytics, and stepwise implementation with a Data & Analytics Center of Excellence. Novel functions such as offline work on the app, interfaces that are meaningful in the environment, and AI-powered insights are attuned to the needs of users in urban and even rural settings. To be effective in the nation of Ghana, leaders must build capacity, prevent unethical use, and revisit regularly so that they get clear, valuable data that will inform better education policy.

On October 15, 2025, the University of Alberta hosted a high level Roundtable on the Future of Canada-China Relations, bringing together leading voices from academia, government and industry to evaluate Canada's position across three domains: trade, technology and innovation, and peace and security. The discussion revealed a complex and contested landscape, marked by interdependence, rising authoritarianism and the erosion of multilateral institutions. Experts grappled with key dilemmas, from the severity of technology risks to the challenge of navigating two increasingly assertive superpowers. This brief distills seven strategic takeaways to guide Canadian policymakers, businesses and civil society as they chart pragmatic course through the next phase of Canada-China relations.

detail.abstract:
In July 2025, we conducted a study with 935 participants on consumer willingness to
pay for cucumbers in Lexington, Kentucky. 

We find that the more expensive a cucumber, the less consumers are willing to buy a cucumber. At USD 2 to 2.5 per slicing cucumber, buyers and non-buyers are nearly evenly split (53 percent vs. 47 percent). Price and minimal pesticide use are key attributes for consumers across age groups. Nearly half of consumers (45 percent) say price is a key factor, while 36 percent care a lot about fewer pesticides and 34 percent prioritize cucumbers with no pesticides at all. Most respondents are highly concerned about pesticides during production (36 percent) and residues on food (50 percent), while concern and knowledge about plastics, especially in production are much lower (14 percent). 

Highlighting the reduction in pesticide use from protective netting and clarifying that extra plastic is only used in production can help researchers and producers anticipate consumer preferences and

title: National Context as a Predictor of Workplace Ostracism: A Meta-Analysis Integrating Organizational and Vocational Perspectives

detail.title: National Context as a Predictor of Workplace Ostracism: A Meta-Analysis Integrating Organizational and Vocational Perspectives
detail.abstract: Workplace ostracism is a pervasive relational stressor that threatens employees’ sense of inclusion, dignity, and psychological well-being, with implications for both organizational functioning and vocational experiences. Although the antecedents and outcomes of ostracism have been widely investigated, less is known about how its prevalence varies across broader contextual factors. To address this gap, we conducted a meta-analysis of mean-level workplace ostracism and tested national context as a potential predictor using random-effects meta-regression. The results revealed substantial cross-country variation, indicating that culturally rooted interpersonal norms significantly shape baseline levels of ostracism in organizations. While the COVID-19 pandemic introduced notable shifts in work arrangements, its direct role in explaining ostracism levels was limited compared to national differences. These findings highlight the importance of cultural and contextual influences in understanding the relational environments within which employees work and build their careers. Implications for organizational behavior, vocational research, and future cross-cultural scholarship are discussed.

detail.title: LLM-powered Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicles Management in Last-mile Transportation
detail.abstract: Heterogeneous autonomous vehicles (HAV) offer a promising approach to providing flexible and efficient last-mile transportation services. A significant challenge, however, is to achieve adaptive fleet composition and dispatching that accounts for dynamic time periods, real-time demand, and varying spatial distributions. Traditional methods often struggle with the complexity and real-time nature of these operational factors. This study proposes a novel framework that integrates a large language model (LLM) with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to address the joint optimization of adaptive fleet composition and real-time vehicle dispatching in HAV management. First, the LLM acts as a strategic determiner to select an effective vehicle mix for different service periods, offering greater adaptability compared to traditional static optimization models. Second, the LLM functions as an adaptive reward designer, generating explicit and context-aware reward functions to guide the DRL agent's training process for vehicle dispatching. To mitigate the risk of AI hallucination and ensure reliable outputs, a hybrid LLM+Rule-based architecture is developed that features a hierarchical prompt parsing module. A memory module is additionally designed to improve computational efficiency by decoupling the LLM inference process from the DRL training loop. Extensive numerical experiments and a real-world case study are conducted across diverse demand scenarios. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DRL, heuristic, and exact solution methods in both solution quality and computational time. These findings underscore the effectiveness of integrating an LLM to achieve adaptive fleet composition and efficient HAV dispatching.

title: The Imitation Game: A Study in Corporate Mimicry

detail.title: The Imitation Game: A Study in Corporate Mimicry
detail.abstract: This paper examines how companies in Uganda imitate competitors as a strategy for survival. It explores two main forms of imitation: neighbor imitation and challenger imitation. Neighbor imitation occurs when firms copy rivals that share similar characteristics such as size, customers, or market structures. Challenger imitation happens when leaders copy smaller or faster competitors that pose a threat to their market position. The study uses examples from Uganda's telecommunications, banking, and fintech sectors, focusing on cases such as MTN and Airtel. These examples show how imitation supports rapid adaptation in volatile markets. The paper argues that imitation is not a sign of weakness, but a deliberate form of learning and risk management. Firms that balance both types of imitation build stronger strategic awareness and resilience. The findings highlight that in unstable markets, success depends on observation, speed, and flexibility. Leaders who learn from competitors maintain relevance and protect their market positions. The paper concludes that imitation, when applied strategically, is a practical and underused tool for sustaining competitive advantage in emerging economies.

detail.abstract: This paper advances Creative Capital Expenditure (CCE) as a framework explaining how creativity performs a capital function for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operating under liquidity constraints. Addressing the question of why creativity matters for SME growth, the paper proposes that feeling foreshadows finance: emotional and cultural resonance create psychological liquidity that later converts into commercial return. A sequential mixed-method study of 101 Afro-Caribbean entrepreneurs in South London shows how emotive, distinctive, and culturally fluent creativity generates trust, memorability, and legitimacy without proportionate financial spend. These relational assets predict commercial performance, indicating what creativity does in constrained environments stabilising growth during scarcity and amplifying profitability when liquidity returns. The study contributes a behavioural-economic explanation for creativity’s role in SME growth and offers implications for entrepreneurs, agencies, and policymakers. Creativity is not a substitute for finance, but its renewable ally, enabling disproportionate outcomes under constraint.

title: The Business Chessboard Strategy (BCS): A Conceptual Framework for AI-Driven Marketing

detail.title: The Business Chessboard Strategy (BCS): A Conceptual Framework for AI-Driven Marketing
detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping marketing strategy, offering unparalleled opportunities for personalization, automation, and strategic foresight. However, existing research often treats AI as a set of tools rather than as an integrated managerial paradigm, leaving a conceptual gap between technological capabilities and strategic frameworks. To address this gap, this paper develops the Business Chessboard Strategy (BCS)—a conceptual model that interprets organizational strategy through the metaphor and logic of chess. Drawing upon secondary insights from recent studies and professional observations in AI-driven marketing, the BCS framework maps key organizational dimensions to chess pieces: King (vision and mission), Queen (core strategy), Rooks (processes and systems), Bishops(culture and ethics), Knights (innovation), and Pawns (operational actions). Through this metaphorical structure, the BCS integrates strategic foresight, decision-making agility, and ethical responsibility into a unified framework for navigating the complexities of AI-enhanced marketing environments. The paper contributes conceptually by bridging metaphor theory, AI strategy, and management practice, providing a flexible framework that can guide both academic inquiry and managerial decision-making in the era of intelligent technologies.

Updated version (October 2025): The paper has been reframed as a conceptual model development study, focusing on theoretical synthesis rather than empirical data collection. The BCS framework is now presented as a conceptual contribution to AI-driven strategic management.

detail.abstract: This tentative abstract is based on a research project examining the singer Saint Levant as a representative figure of cultural entrepreneurship in the contemporary platform-mediated music industry. His trajectory illustrates how multilingual expression, diasporic identity, and curated aesthetics function as strategic resources for value creation within digital ecosystems where attention, narrative coherence, and community participation replace traditional gatekeeping. Through a blend of English, French, and Arabic, Saint Levant converts hybridity into a distinctive market proposition capable of resonating across geographies and cultural codes. His brand operates as an integrated system in which music, visual semiotics, and personal discourse reinforce one another, generating a form of symbolic capital that sustains both audience engagement and diversified monetization. The case highlights the managerial tensions associated with scaling such an identity-rich enterprise, including authenticity management, governance choices, and the evaluation of potential partnerships. It also provides the conceptual premises for the emerging notion of Hybrid Identity Marketing, a framework that interprets cultural hybridity as a core driver of contemporary branding strategies. title: The Impact of JSON-LD Metadata on ChatGPT Visibility

detail.title: The Impact of JSON-LD Metadata on ChatGPT Visibility

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This study examines whether implementing structured metadata (JSON-LD Schema.org markup) on websites can improve a business’s visibility in ChatGPT responses. We focus on real estate agencies as a case study, analyzing which site attributes correlate with an agency being “known” or referenced by ChatGPT.

Methods: We gathered public data on 1,508 real estate agents in Germany and identified which of these agents ChatGPT could provide information about (indicating ChatGPT visibility). For each agent’s website, we recorded the presence of Schema.org metadata (FAQPage, Organization, Product schemas), as well as SEO/technical factors like mobile optimization, robots.txt, sitemap, headings usage, image alt-text, internal links, and page load speed. A logistic regression was used to determine which factors significantly predict ChatGPT visibility, controlling for other variables.

Results: Agents whose websites included FAQPage schema markup were far more likely to be visible on ChatGPT (6.2% of visible agents had FAQ schema vs. only 0.8% of non-visible; p = 0.002). Presence of Product schema (e.g. schema for listings or services) also strongly correlated with visibility (17.2% vs 1.8%; p < 0.001). Key technical SEO features were likewise more common among ChatGPT-visible agents: nearly all had mobile-friendly sites (99.0% vs 88.8% of non-visible; p < 0.001) and a robots.txt file (92.3% vs 80.6%; p < 0.001). Visible agents’ sites were more likely to use structured headings (94.7% had an <h2> vs 74.4% of non-visible; 86.6% had an <h3> vs 61.4% of non-visible; p < 0.001), and their pages loaded faster on average (418 ms vs 623 ms; p = 0.014). A multivariate logistic regression confirmed FAQPage schema as the strongest positive predictor of ChatGPT visibility (odds ratio ≈ 13, p < 0.001), followed by Product schema (OR ≈ 4, p < 0.001). Other significant factors included mobile optimization (OR ≈ 5.2, p = 0.026), presence of a robots.txt (OR ≈ 3.4, p < 0.001), and the use of multiple heading levels (having <h2>: OR ≈ 3.3; <h3>: OR ≈ 2.3; both p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Our findings provide empirical support that adding Schema.org metadata – particularly FAQ schemas that supply question-answer pairs – is associated with significantly higher chances of being recognized or cited by AI chat systems like ChatGPT. In practice, this suggests that businesses can improve their AI-driven visibility by adopting structured data and following strong SEO practices. We discuss the implications for “Generative Engine Optimization” (GEO) and estimate the potential monetary benefits of increased AI visibility, which can be substantial given the high client value in real estate.

detail.abstract: Health programmes designed to improve access to essential medicines continue to experience implementation challenges in many low-and middle-income countries. Despite strong policy intentions, persistent failures arise from weaknesses in programme design, system capacity, and patient-level barriers. This paper examines the underlying reasons for these failures within medicine access initiatives. Methods: A narrative synthesis approach was used to review peer-reviewed literature from 2017 to 2024 on health systems performance, medicine access models, implementation science, workforce constraints, and social determinants of health. Evidence was drawn from global health, health policy, and health service research sources to identify common patterns of programmatic failure. Results: Across the reviewed evidence, five recurring drivers of programme failure emerged: (1) misalignment between programme design and frontline realities; (2) supply-chain fragilities and poor governance; (3) workforce shortages and implementation fatigue; (4) weak digital and data systems hampering continuity of care; and (5) patient-level barriers shaped by social and economic determinants. These interacting factors create systemic bottlenecks that limit programme fidelity, sustainability, and equity. Findings: The synthesis highlights that medicine access programmes fail not because the model is flawed, but because health systems lack the resilience, resources, and adaptive capacity needed for effective delivery. Programmes that embed frontline participation, strengthen governance structures, support digital readiness, and incorporate patient-centred approaches demonstrate better performance. Conclusion: Strengthening medicine access initiatives requires addressing upstream system constraints, investing in workforce capacity, improving supply-chain reliability, and designing models that reflect both implementer and patient realities. A systems-oriented, adaptive, and equity-driven approach is essential to ensure consistent and sustainable access to chronic medicines in resource-constrained settings.

title: Evaluating Individual Contributions in Ugandan Businesses: Navigating the Performance Non-Separability Problem

detail.title: Evaluating Individual Contributions in Ugandan Businesses: Navigating the Performance Non-Separability Problem
detail.abstract: A central challenge in team-based organizations is the performance non-separability problem-the difficulty of evaluating individual contributions when only collective output is observable. This issue is particularly acute in resourceconstrained contexts like Uganda, where formal performance metrics are often unavailable. This paper explores how supervisors in Ugandan businesses navigate this dilemma, drawing on the theoretical lens of covariance-based inference (Uribe et al., 2022). We argue that in the absence of direct data, supervisors rely on counterfactual reasoning, inferring individual productivity by observing how team performance fluctuates with changes in membership. Through qualitative analysis of sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, and services, we identify two key factors that strengthen this inferential process: frequent employee rotation and clearly defined hierarchical authority. Rotation across teams creates natural experiments, providing supervisors with the variation needed to isolate individual impact. Meanwhile, employees in high-authority roles attract greater evaluative attention, making their contributions more perceptible. The findings suggest that instead of importing complex performance measurement systems, managers in similar contexts can enhance evaluation accuracy by strategically leveraging organic workplace dynamics. We propose practical implications, including the formalization of rotation practices, training for supervisors on implicit inference, and a heightened awareness of perceptual management by employees. This paper contributes to the understanding of subjective performance appraisal by theorizing it as a rational, inference-based process grounded in the observable realities of team production.

title: High-Level Specification of MILP Problems with Class Diagrams and Graph Transformations: A Case Study in Model-Driven Optimisation of the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Problem

detail.title: High-Level Specification of MILP Problems with Class Diagrams and Graph Transformations: A Case Study in Model-Driven Optimisation of the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Problem
detail.abstract: The Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Competition (IHTC) 2024 presented the Integrated Healthcare Timetabling Problem (IHTP), a challenging resource-allocation problem in the healthcare domain. This paper introduces an accessible novel specification and solution approach to the IHTP based on modelling domain concepts via Unified Modeling Language (UML) class diagrams, defining domain constraints via the Object Constraint Language (OCL), and declaring decision variables via graph transformation rules. Our method captures all hard and soft constraints of the IHTP directly in domain terminology. We used the Graph-Based (M)ILP Problem Specification (GIPS) tool to demonstrate one possibility for systematically translating our problem specification into a Model-Driven Optimisation (MDO) solution that can optimise IHTP instances with Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). A key advantage of this approach lies in its flexibility: Solution variants can be explored by simply adding or removing constraints or objective terms without manually adjusting solver-related implementation code. Our GIPS-based implementation solves all 30 benchmark instances within the 10 min time limit. With a relaxed time limit, two of the public IHTC instances were solved to optimality. While the current workflow involves some manual translation before processing instances with GIPS, these steps are largely systematic and lend themselves to automation. We, therefore, aim to develop a fully automated pipeline in future work.

detail.abstract: The Washington Consensus has been one of the most influential and controversial economic policy paradigms of the late 20th century. Conceived as a ten-point decalogue of market-oriented reforms, its implementation generated a vast body of literature evaluating its impacts. This qualitative narrative review synthesizes evidence from 53 academic studies to offer a panoramic view of its legacy. It explores its origins and evolution, the empirical evidence associating it with improvements in growth, and the criticisms linking it to rising inequality and economic crises. Finally, it analyzes the emergence of post-consensus narratives, arguing that this evolution, rather than a rupture, represents a strategic adaptation of neoliberalism. The findings reveal that while the era of universal solutions is over, the post-consensus paradigm often recycles fundamental principles under a new language of inclusion and contextual specificity, posing new challenges for the search for genuine development alternatives.

detail.abstract: Marketing has always been an art-shaping stories, relationships, and perceptions. But in today's era of macroeconomic uncertainty, digital acceleration, and intensifying competition, marketing must also become a science: a rigorous, AI-enabled engine for national growth and economic resilience. Traditional approaches like last-click attribution no longer provide a reliable source of truth for measuring performance for marketers. detail.abstract: PurposeIncident learning is key to improving clinical quality and safety. This study evaluates the impact of workflow changes related to increasing remote work on incident learning in a radiation oncology clinic. Methods and MaterialsWe analyzed reported event data for three 12-month intervals: pre-COVID (March 1, 2019 – February 29, 2020), during-COVID (March 1, 2020 – February 28, 2021), and COVID-adapted (March 1, 2021 – February 28, 2022). Events were prospectively analyzed by our multi-disciplinary Quality and Safety Committee using an electronic incident learning system capture system. We evaluated event reporting rates, severity, contributing factors, point of event origin and detection. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used to compare characteristics between the three time intervals.ResultsOver the three years considered, 798 event reports were submitted and reviewed.  The reporting rate (number of reported events per patient simulated) decreased over time: pre-COVID 0.18 [335/1834]; during-COVID 0.15 [245/1609]; and COVID-adapted 0.13 [218/1695]. The severity of events declined over time (p=<0.001). As time progressed, the location of event origin shifted towards earlier steps in our workflows (i.e. towards simulation-related imaging and treatment planning).  Similarly, the point of event discovery shifted to earlier steps as well (ie. towards during pretreatment review and verification, and away from treatment delivery and management). Communication was frequently identified as a contributor during the latter two time periods while workload was less frequently cited compared to pre-COVID. ConclusionThe severity, site of origin/discovery of events and contributing factors varied over time demonstrating shifts in the nature of events associated with changes in pandemic-induced workflows. Additional efforts to promote incident reporting are needed to maintain the benefits of incident learning.

This effect is observed in a range of industries, modeled by several authors and various remedies have been suggested. Most of the authors explore the cause of bullwhip effect. In this paper, the impact of push and pull marketing strategies on bullwhip effect has been explored. The bullwhip effect starts at the retailers end and its effect lasts upto the point of suppliers. Furthermore, this paper also explores the optimal order quantity for retailers under certain conditions, in case of pull marketing strategies such that the total cost per unit time at retailer's end is minimum. A mathematical model has been developed suggesting the situations under which a supplier takes the decision about whether to fill the order or not. By eliminating or controlling this effect, it is possible to increase product profitability, reducing the useless costs such as stock-out and obsolescence costs.

detail.abstract: This study maps the scholarly landscape of survivability, resiliency, and sustainability in small independent retailers (SIRs) and proposes a targeted research agenda. A hybrid review was conducted, combining systematic retrieval from Scopus (n = 150 documents), bibliometric analysis, and qualitative content analysis. The bibliometric analysis combined the performance indicators of publications and citations with the VOS-based science mapping of abstracts topic. The content analysis involved methodological coding and agenda mapping with high intercoder reliability, using the research onion model and inductive agenda development. Publication activity has increased markedly since 2018. Topic mapping highlights digital transformation, policy ecosystems, local market dynamics, and empirical strategy. Methodologically, positivist mono-method quantitative designs prevail, whereas mixed-method and longitudinal approaches are underutilized. This study classifies 12 research agendas across survivability (3), resiliency (5), and sustainability (4), along with related methodologies, topics, regions, and sustainable development goal (SDG) coverage. Key gaps include the need for longitudinal designs, complex mixed methods, crossregional comparisons, and stronger integration of policy and action research. This study provides the first holistic synthesis linking survivability, resiliency, and sustainability in SIRs, offering a validated agenda taxonomy, methodologically grounded recommendations, and SDG-aligned priorities to guide future research and policymaking.

detail.abstract: Despite their promise in promoting healthy behavior, wearable self-tracking devices often fall short of long-term effectiveness due to negative user experiences. This study adopts a coping-theoretic perspective to explore how users respond to negative incidents. Drawing on narrative data from 62 longterm users of wearable self-tracking devices in Switzerland, the analysis identifies different categories of coping: Proactive coping involves anticipatory strategies aimed at preventing incidents, such as cognitive reinterpretation, seeking social support, cheating and manipulating information, and selective use. Reactive coping emerged in two subcategories: Avoidant-reactive coping includes responses after an incident has occurred aimed at disengagement, denial, and distancing, including rationalizing and downplaying the incident, doubting and dismissing the wearable, or discontinuing use. Ameliorativereactive coping also includes post-incident responses but aimed at adaptation and constructive engagement, leading to improvement of personal outcomes, such as changing one's behavior or adapting use practices. The study contributes to the information systems coping literature by extending ways of coping and introducing ameliorative-reactive coping as a novel category. It also contributes to wearable-specific research by offering a coping-informed explanation for high attrition and inconsistent usage patterns. Finally, the study provides practical insights for designers and providers of wearables.

These results suggest that healthy aging can meaningfully bolster labor supply and productivity among older workers, mitigating demographic headwinds for growth and public finances.

detail.title: DrugAgent: A Theory-Driven LLM Multi-Agent System for Automating Machine Learning Programming in Drug Discovery
detail.abstract: Drug discovery is a costly, decade-long process characterized by high uncertainty and frequent failure. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer the potential to accelerate early discovery stages by reducing trial-and-error and leveraging large-scale biological and chemical data. Yet, constructing reliable machine learning (ML) pipelines for drug discovery remains difficult because the process spans multiple domains and requires deep integration of specialized knowledge. We propose DrugAgent, a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework that automates machine learning programming for drug discovery tasks. The architecture is guided by theories of teamwork and innovation in organizational science, particularly division of cognitive labor, cognitive diversity, knowledge integration, and iterative learning. DrugAgent comprises two collaborating agents: a Planner, which manages idea-space exploration, and an Instructor, which executes domain-aware implementations using a codified repository of biomedical knowledge. Experiments demonstrate that DrugAgent outperforms existing agentic systems and achieves accuracy comparable to expert-designed pipelines while exhibiting higher reliability. Beyond technical gains, this study demonstrates how foundational theories of human collaboration can inform the design of intelligent systems for scientific research. We contribute to both practice and theory by offering an architecture that accelerates AI-driven discovery and a conceptual bridge linking organizational learning with autonomous LLM agent teamwork.

detail.title: The Role of AI, IoT and Blockchain in Enabling Workplace Sustainability and Efficiency-an Empirical Analysis
detail.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and Blockchain has revolutionized organizational working practices, enabling digital transformation and sustainability. The current study investigates the drivers of the adoption of these technologies, analyzes their impact on the productivity of employees. There is evidence that AI-powered automation boosts efficiency through minimization of repetitive tasks, IoT optimizes the use of resources, and Blockchain brings transparency and security to business processes. AI-powered system resistance, lack of training in AI, and security risks in data collection, however, are impediments to adoption. The findings of factor analysis reveal four critical factors that shape the adoption of AI: efficiency, collaboration, automation, and work flexibility. The ANOVA findings show that attitudes toward AI-powered up skilling are not statistically influenced by AI-powered system resistance, which means other factors aside from those related to AI may have more importance. The study offers relevant insights for organizations functioning in emerging economies. This research contributes valuable knowledge to the convergence of technology adoption and sustainable digital transformation, providing strategic guidance to organizations on how to adopt AI, IoT, and Blockchain, while avoiding pitfalls in their adoption. The research highlights the significance of responsible integration of AI, employee participation, and ethical aspects to realize the full potential of these technologies in contemporary workplaces.

detail.abstract: We present the ENV-FIBA macro-micro model framework that can be used to analyze the climate-macro-financial consequences of climate scenarios and related policy counterfactuals. The model consists of a multi-country Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) core and a connected micro simulation module for an economy’s individual nonfinancial firms and banks. The climate-macro-financial scenario simulations are anchored in future temperature and emission pathways, alongside policy assumptions regarding carbon taxation, fiscal revenue recycling and reinvestment, optional carbon border adjustment mechanisms, and others. We illustrate the use of the model for Japan. We emphasize, exemplify with the model, and recommend in general: (1) that physical and transition risk effects be modeled jointly to a maximal extent (given their intertwined nature); (2) that it is important to consider bank balance sheets that are dynamic (not static), to capture the differential growth of emmission intensive industries that may shrink, opposed to those that may flourish; and (3) related to the latter, that such dynamically evolving lending has primary impacts on bank solvency via interest income, along with quantitatively often smaller impacts through loan losses from borrower defaults.

title: Why Democracy Should Be Replaced by AI Algorithms: The Case for Algorithmic Governance

detail.title: Why Democracy Should Be Replaced by AI Algorithms: The Case for Algorithmic Governance
detail.abstract: This paper presents a provocative and evidence-based argument for the systematic replacement of traditional democratic processes with a system of algorithmic governance. We contend that human-led democracy, with its inherent cognitive biases, susceptibility to misinformation, and slow decision-making processes, is no longer adequate for governing complex modern societies. We propose a framework where key policy decisions are delegated to a network of specialized AI systems, governed by a transparent, ethically-grounded constitution. This system, we argue, would lead to more rational, efficient, and equitable outcomes than current democratic models. We address the profound ethical and practical challenges of such a transition, including the potential for algorithmic bias and the erosion of human agency, and offer a roadmap for a phased implementation that prioritizes public trust and accountability.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the impact of fiscal policy on inflation expectations across a large sample of advanced economies (AEs) and emerging market economies (EMs). We identify episodes of significant fiscal adjustment using both quantitative thresholds and a narrative approach and find that such episodes are associated with statistically significant changes in inflation expectations in EMs while the responses are muted in AEs. We also document that the relationship between fiscal policy and inflation expectations is more pronounced in high-inflation environments and under weak fiscal positions. Additionally, we explore how market perceptions of sovereign risk, as well as monetary and exchange rate frameworks, influence the transmission of fiscal policy to inflation expectations. Our empirical results suggest that it is especially important for EMs to implement prudent fiscal policy as it may help reduce inflationary pressures and inflation expectations.

title: The Latent Role of Open Models in the AI Economy

detail.title: The Latent Role of Open Models in the AI Economy
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of large language models (LLMs) is mediated by an emerging market for AI inference. However, its economic structure is poorly understood due to challenges in measuring LLM usage. While some fear AI will inevitably evolve into an oligopolistic structure with winner-take-most dynamics, others argue that the rapid emergence of capable open models will inevitably commoditize AI inference. Leveraging data on model-level usage and prices from OpenRouter comprising just under 1% of the total market for LLM inference, we empirically uncover the latent role of open models relative to closed models. Closed models dominate, with on average 80% of monthly LLM tokens using closed models despite much higher prices - on average 6x the price of open models - and only modest performance advantages. Frontier open models typically reach performance parity with frontier closed models within months, suggesting relatively fast convergence. Nevertheless, users continue to select closed models even when open alternatives are cheaper and offer superior performance. This systematic underutilization is economically significant: reallocating demand from observably dominated closed models to superior open models would reduce average prices by over 70% and, when extrapolated to the total market, generate an estimated $24.8 billion in additional consumer savings across 2025. These results suggest that closed model dominance reflects powerful drivers beyond model capabilities and price - whether switching costs, brand loyalty, or information frictions - with the economic magnitude of these hidden factors proving far larger than previously recognized, reframing open models as a largely latent, but high-potential, source of value in the AI economy.
